BoardPart 0 · Math toolkit

Learning board · Maths · Part 0

Math toolkit

The math that economics courses in Germany build on: rules of arithmetic, equations and functions, derivatives, curve sketching, functions of several variables, and the growth-rate tools macroeconomics uses all the time. Topics 0.7 to 0.10, on the Micro board, add the tools that the Mikroökonomie I tasks need. Work through it once, then come back whenever a calculation gets stuck.

German terms included

Every topic gives the German term next to the English one (Ableitung for derivative, Nullstelle for zero), so it matches your lecture, your Formelsammlung, and German exam questions.

Every curve is computed

Each graph is drawn from the formula next to it. Move a slider and the graph, the readouts, and the worked formula update together.

Notation

The board writes a decimal point; German exams write a decimal comma (0.5 is 0,5). \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm, \(\lg\) the logarithm to base 10.

FormulaFractions, brackets, binomials

Order of operations: brackets first, then powers, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction (Klammer vor Potenz vor Punkt vor Strich).

Fractions (Bruchrechnung)

\[ \frac{a}{b} + \frac{c}{d} = \frac{ad + bc}{bd} \qquad \frac{a}{b}\cdot\frac{c}{d} = \frac{ac}{bd} \] \[ \frac{a}{b} : \frac{c}{d} = \frac{a}{b}\cdot\frac{d}{c} \]

Binomial formulas (Binomische Formeln)

\[ (a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2 \] \[ (a-b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2 \] \[ (a+b)(a-b) = a^2 - b^2 \]

Brackets (Klammern)

\[ a\,(b + c) = ab + ac \qquad -(a - b) = -a + b \]
FormulaSum sign

Sum sign (Summenzeichen)

\[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i = x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_n \] \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} c\,x_i = c\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \] \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i + y_i) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i + \sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i \] \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n} c = n\,c \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \]

Nominal GDP is such a sum over all final goods: \(\$Y = \sum_i p_i\,q_i\), the price times the quantity of each good.

FormulaPowers and roots

Powers (Potenzgesetze)

\[ a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n} \qquad \frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n} \] \[ (a^m)^n = a^{m \cdot n} \qquad (ab)^n = a^n\,b^n \] \[ a^0 = 1 \qquad a^{-n} = \frac{1}{a^n} \]

Roots (Wurzeln), for \(a, b \ge 0\)

\[ \sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n} \qquad \sqrt[n]{a^m} = a^{m/n} \] \[ \sqrt{a}\cdot\sqrt{b} = \sqrt{ab} \]

Write roots as powers with fractional exponents before you simplify or take a derivative: \(\sqrt{x} = x^{1/2}\) and \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-1/2}\).

FormulaLogarithms

Definition

\[ \log_a x = y \iff a^y = x \] \[ \ln x = \log_e x, \qquad e \approx 2.71828 \]

Log rules (Logarithmengesetze), for \(x, y > 0\)

\[ \ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y \qquad \ln\frac{x}{y} = \ln x - \ln y \] \[ \ln(x^r) = r \ln x \qquad \ln 1 = 0 \qquad \ln e = 1 \] \[ e^{\ln x} = x \qquad \ln(e^x) = x \qquad \log_a x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln a} \]

Logs pull an unknown out of the exponent. At 2% growth a year, output doubles when \(1.02^t = 2\), so \(t = \ln 2 / \ln 1.02 \approx 35\) years.

PitfallsCommon mistakes (typische Fehler)
WrongRight
\((a+b)^2 = a^2 + b^2\)\((a+b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\)
\(\sqrt{a+b} = \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}\)\(\sqrt{a+b}\) cannot be split
\(\ln(a+b) = \ln a + \ln b\)\(\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b\)
\(\dfrac{1}{a+b} = \dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b}\)\(\dfrac{1}{a} + \dfrac{1}{b} = \dfrac{a+b}{ab}\)
\(\dfrac{a+b}{a} = b\)\(\dfrac{a+b}{a} = 1 + \dfrac{b}{a}\)
\(-2^2 = 4\)\(-2^2 = -4,\quad (-2)^2 = 4\)
\(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m n}\)\(a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}\)
\(\dfrac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m/n}\)\(\dfrac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}\)

Cancel only factors, never single terms of a sum. German students learn it as "Aus Summen kürzen nur die Dummen."

FormulaLinear functions and systems

Linear function (lineare Funktion)

\[ y = m\,x + n \]

\(m\) is the slope (Steigung): the change in \(y\) when \(x\) rises by 1. \(n\) is the intercept (y-Achsenabschnitt): the value of \(y\) at \(x = 0\).

Slope from two points, and the zero (Nullstelle)

\[ m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} \qquad x_0 = -\frac{n}{m} \]

Two equations, two unknowns (lineares Gleichungssystem)

\[ p = a - b\,x \quad\text{and}\quad p = c + d\,x \] \[ a - b\,x = c + d\,x \;\Rightarrow\; x^* = \frac{a - c}{b + d} \]

Setting both right-hand sides equal is the Gleichsetzungsverfahren. Economists put the price on the vertical axis, so demand and supply are usually written as \(p\) in terms of \(x\) (Preis-Absatz-Funktion).

FormulaQuadratic equations

pq-Formel

\[ x^2 + p\,x + q = 0 \] \[ x_{1,2} = -\frac{p}{2} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{p}{2}\right)^2 - q} \]

abc-Formel (Mitternachtsformel)

\[ a\,x^2 + b\,x + c = 0 \] \[ x_{1,2} = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} \]
  • Divide by \(a\) before you use the pq-Formel: the \(x^2\) term needs the coefficient 1.
  • The term under the root (Diskriminante) decides: positive gives two solutions, zero gives one, negative gives none.
  • Example: \(2x^2 - 8x + 6 = 0\) becomes \(x^2 - 4x + 3 = 0\). Then \(x = 2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 3}\), so \(x = 1\) or \(x = 3\).
GraphSolving two linear equations

Demand \(p = a - b\,x\) and supply \(p = c + d\,x\). The solution of the system is where the two lines cross. Dashed lines show where you started.

FormulaExponential and log functions

Exponential function (Exponentialfunktion)

\[ f(x) = e^x, \qquad e^x > 0, \qquad e^0 = 1 \]

Natural log (Logarithmusfunktion)

\[ g(x) = \ln x, \qquad x > 0, \qquad \ln 1 = 0 \]

Constant growth at rate \(g\): yearly and continuous

\[ X_t = X_0\,(1+g)^t \qquad X_t = X_0\,e^{g t} \]
  • \(\ln x\) is the inverse (Umkehrfunktion) of \(e^x\): one undoes the other.
  • \(\ln x\) exists only for \(x > 0\) (Definitionsbereich). Check this first in every exercise with a log.
  • Logs turn constant growth into a straight line: \(\ln X_t = \ln X_0 + t\,\ln(1+g)\). That is why long GDP series are plotted on a log scale.
IdeaThe slope at a point

The derivative (Ableitung) \(f'(x)\) is the slope of the tangent (Tangente) at \(x\): how fast \(f\) changes when \(x\) changes a little. It is what the slope of a secant (Sekante) through two points turns into when the two points move together.

  • Marginal means derivative. Marginal cost (Grenzkosten) is \(K'(x)\), marginal revenue (Grenzerlös) is \(E'(x)\), and the marginal propensity to consume (marginale Konsumquote) is \(dC/dY\).
  • \(f'(x) > 0\): \(f\) rises (steigend). \(f'(x) < 0\): \(f\) falls (fallend).
  • The second derivative \(f''(x)\) is the slope of the slope. \(f'' > 0\): convex, curved upward (linksgekrümmt). \(f'' < 0\): concave, curved downward (rechtsgekrümmt).
FormulaWorked examples

Power and sum rule

\[ f(x) = 3x^4 - 2x + 7 \;\Rightarrow\; f'(x) = 12x^3 - 2 \]

Root as a power

\[ f(x) = \sqrt{x} = x^{1/2} \] \[ f'(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,x^{-1/2} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \]

Product rule and chain rule

\[ f(x) = x\,e^{2x} \] \[ f'(x) = 1 \cdot e^{2x} + x \cdot 2e^{2x} = (1 + 2x)\,e^{2x} \]

Chain rule with a log

\[ f(x) = \ln(1 + x^2) \;\Rightarrow\; f'(x) = \frac{2x}{1 + x^2} \]

Quotient rule

\[ f(x) = \frac{x}{x+1} \] \[ f'(x) = \frac{1\cdot(x+1) - x \cdot 1}{(x+1)^2} = \frac{1}{(x+1)^2} \]
FormulaDerivative rules (Ableitungsregeln)

Definition (Differentialquotient)

\[ f'(x) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h} \]

Power, factor, and sum rule

\[ (x^n)' = n\,x^{n-1} \qquad (c)' = 0 \] \[ (c\,f)' = c\,f' \qquad (f + g)' = f' + g' \]

Product rule (Produktregel)

\[ (f\,g)' = f'\,g + f\,g' \]

Quotient rule (Quotientenregel)

\[ \left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \frac{f'\,g - f\,g'}{g^2} \]

Chain rule (Kettenregel): outer times inner derivative

\[ \bigl(f(g(x))\bigr)' = f'\bigl(g(x)\bigr)\cdot g'(x) \]

Learn by heart

\[ (e^x)' = e^x \qquad (\ln x)' = \frac{1}{x} \qquad (a^x)' = a^x \ln a \]

L'Hospital's rule (Regel von L'Hospital): limits of the form 0/0

\[ \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)} \quad \text{if } f(a) = g(a) = 0 \]

Example: CRRA utility (Makro 3.6, Aufgabe 4.4.9), differentiate with respect to σ

\[ \begin{aligned} \lim_{\sigma \to 1} \frac{C^{1-\sigma} - 1}{1-\sigma} &= \lim_{\sigma \to 1} \frac{-C^{1-\sigma}\ln C}{-1} \\ &= \ln C \end{aligned} \]
GraphFrom secant to tangent

Shrink the step \(h\) and the secant through \(P\) and \(Q\) turns into the tangent at \(P\). Its slope turns into the derivative \(f'(x_0)\).

IdeaCurve sketching step by step

Kurvendiskussion means working out the shape of a function from its derivatives. Exams ask for the same steps every time.

  1. Domain (Definitionsbereich): where is \(f\) defined? A log needs a positive argument, and a denominator must not be zero.
  2. Zeros (Nullstellen): solve \(f(x) = 0\).
  3. Extremes (Extremstellen): the necessary condition (notwendige Bedingung) is \(f'(x) = 0\). The sufficient condition (hinreichende Bedingung) is \(f''(x) < 0\) for a maximum (Hochpunkt) and \(f''(x) > 0\) for a minimum (Tiefpunkt).
  4. Inflection points (Wendepunkte): \(f''(x) = 0\) and \(f'''(x) \neq 0\). The curvature switches there.
  5. Monotonicity and curvature: the signs of \(f'\) and \(f''\) between those points.
  6. Behavior at the edges: what \(f\) does at the ends of the domain, for example as \(x \to \infty\).

The same steps find optimal decisions. Profit is highest where marginal revenue equals marginal cost: \(G'(x) = E'(x) - K'(x) = 0\).

FormulaProfit maximum, worked through

Revenue, cost, profit (Erlös, Kosten, Gewinn)

\[ E(x) = p\,x \qquad K(x) = 0.1x^3 - 1.2x^2 + 6x + 10 \] \[ G(x) = -0.1x^3 + 1.2x^2 + (p - 6)\,x - 10 \]

Necessary condition: price equals marginal cost

\[ G'(x) = p - (0.3x^2 - 2.4x + 6) = 0 \] \[ x^2 - 8x + \left(20 - \tfrac{10}{3}\,p\right) = 0 \] \[ x_{1,2} = 4 \pm \sqrt{\tfrac{10}{3}\,p - 4} \]

Sufficient condition

\[ G''(x) = 2.4 - 0.6\,x < 0 \iff x > 4 \]

The larger solution is the maximum (Hochpunkt) and the smaller one a minimum (Tiefpunkt). \(G''(4) = 0\), so \(x = 4\) is the inflection point at every price. Here \(p\) is the market price; in the pq-Formel step the coefficient of \(x\) is \(-8\). \(K(x)\) is a typical S-shaped cost curve (ertragsgesetzliche Kostenfunktion).

In Mikroökonomie I the same functions are written \(TR(Q)\), \(TC(Q)\), and \(\Pi(Q)\) with quantity \(Q\) and price \(P\). Topic 0.8 uses that notation for the same cost function.

IdeaOne input at a time

Macro models have several inputs at once: output depends on capital and labor, consumption on income and taxes. A partial derivative (partielle Ableitung) changes one input and holds all the others fixed (ceteris paribus).

  • Write \(\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\) or \(f_x\). Treat every other variable as a constant, then use the usual rules.
  • The total differential (totales Differential) adds up the effects of small changes in all inputs. Comparative statics in models like IS-LM works this way.
  • To maximize under a constraint (Optimierung unter Nebenbedingungen), use the Lagrange method. At the optimum, the highest reachable level curve just touches the constraint.
FormulaPartial derivatives

Cobb-Douglas production function

\[ Y = K^{\alpha} N^{1-\alpha}, \qquad 0 < \alpha < 1 \]

Marginal products (Grenzproduktivität)

\[ \frac{\partial Y}{\partial K} = \alpha\,K^{\alpha-1}N^{1-\alpha} = \alpha\,\frac{Y}{K} \] \[ \frac{\partial Y}{\partial N} = (1-\alpha)\,K^{\alpha}N^{-\alpha} = (1-\alpha)\,\frac{Y}{N} \]

Total differential

\[ dY = \frac{\partial Y}{\partial K}\,dK + \frac{\partial Y}{\partial N}\,dN \]

Divide the total differential by \(Y\) and you get growth rates: \(\frac{dY}{Y} = \alpha\,\frac{dK}{K} + (1-\alpha)\,\frac{dN}{N}\). This is where growth accounting starts.

FormulaLagrange method

Problem

\[ \max_{K,\,N}\ K^{\alpha}N^{1-\alpha} \quad \text{subject to} \quad r\,K + w\,N = B \]

Lagrange function (Lagrange-Funktion)

\[ \mathcal{L} = K^{\alpha}N^{1-\alpha} + \lambda\,(B - rK - wN) \]

Set every partial derivative to zero

\[ \mathcal{L}_K = \alpha\,\frac{Y}{K} - \lambda r = 0 \] \[ \mathcal{L}_N = (1-\alpha)\,\frac{Y}{N} - \lambda w = 0 \] \[ \mathcal{L}_\lambda = B - rK - wN = 0 \]

Solution

\[ \frac{(1-\alpha)\,K}{\alpha\,N} = \frac{w}{r} \;\Rightarrow\; K^* = \frac{\alpha B}{r}, \quad N^* = \frac{(1-\alpha)B}{w} \]

Divide the first two conditions to get rid of \(\lambda\), then use the budget. Here \(\lambda\) is the Lagrange multiplier: how much the maximum rises if the budget grows by one unit.

GraphBest mix of capital and labor

A firm spends \(B = 100\) on capital at price \(r\) and labor at wage \(w\). An isoquant (Isoquante) joins all mixes that give the same output. The optimum \(A\) sits where the budget line touches the highest isoquant it can reach.

Output \(Y^*\)5.58

FormulaGrowth rates and approximations

Growth rate (Wachstumsrate)

\[ g_X = \frac{X_t - X_{t-1}}{X_{t-1}} = \frac{\Delta X}{X} \]

Approximations for small \(x\) and \(y\)

\[ (1+x)(1+y) \approx 1 + x + y \qquad \frac{1+x}{1+y} \approx 1 + x - y \] \[ \ln(1+x) \approx x \]

Growth rates of products, ratios, and powers

\[ g_{XY} \approx g_X + g_Y \qquad g_{X/Y} \approx g_X - g_Y \] \[ g_{X^a} \approx a\,g_X \]
  • Real interest rate: \(1 + r = \dfrac{1+i}{1+\pi^e}\), so \(r \approx i - \pi^e\).
  • Real GDP growth is about nominal GDP growth minus inflation.
  • Doubling time is about 70 divided by the growth rate in percent (rule of 70), because \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69\).
  • The approximations are good for rates of a few percent and poor for large ones.
FormulaGrowth rates in continuous time (Wachstumsraten in stetiger Zeit)

Macro models often run in continuous time: \(\dot X = dX/dt\) is the change per moment, and \(\dot X/X\) is the growth rate (Makro 3.5, 3.5.3, 3.6). There the rules for products and ratios hold exactly, not just approximately.

Growth rate as the time derivative of the log

\[ \frac{d \ln X(t)}{dt} = \frac{1}{X(t)}\cdot\frac{dX(t)}{dt} = \frac{\dot X(t)}{X(t)} \]

Products, ratios, and powers (exact)

\[ \ln(XY) = \ln X + \ln Y \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{\dot{(XY)}}{XY} = \frac{\dot X}{X} + \frac{\dot Y}{Y} \] \[ \frac{\dot{(X/Y)}}{X/Y} = \frac{\dot X}{X} - \frac{\dot Y}{Y} \qquad \frac{\dot{(X^a)}}{X^a} = a\,\frac{\dot X}{X} \]

Constant growth at rate \(g\)

\[ X(t) = X_0\,e^{gt} \;\Leftrightarrow\; \ln X(t) = \ln X_0 + g\,t \]
  • Why it works: the log turns products into sums (0.1), and the chain rule gives \(d\ln X/dt = \dot X/X\) (0.3).
  • Example: \(Y = AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}\) gives \(\dot Y/Y = \dot A/A + \alpha\,\dot K/K + (1-\alpha)\,\dot L/L\).
  • Link to discrete time: \(\ln(1+g) \approx g\) for small \(g\), because the slope of \(\ln x\) at \(x = 1\) is 1. So a discrete rate of 8 % per year is a continuous rate of \(\ln 1.08 = 0.077\).
  • On a log scale, constant growth is a straight line with slope \(g\) (Makro 2, Tutorium 4.4.2).
FormulaElasticity (Elastizität)

Elasticity of \(y\) with respect to \(x\)

\[ \varepsilon_{y,x} = \frac{dy/y}{dx/x} = \frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{x}{y} = \frac{d\ln y}{d\ln x} \]
  • Read it as the percent change in \(y\) when \(x\) rises by 1%.
  • \(|\varepsilon| > 1\): elastic (elastisch). \(|\varepsilon| < 1\): inelastic (unelastisch).
  • Power functions have a constant elasticity: \(y = a\,x^b\) gives \(\varepsilon = b\). In \(Y = K^{\alpha}N^{1-\alpha}\), the output elasticity of capital is \(\alpha\).
  • A semi-elasticity \(\frac{d\ln y}{dx}\) gives the percent change in \(y\) per unit of \(x\). Macro uses it for money demand: \(L(i) = \lambda e^{-\kappa i}\) has \(\frac{d\ln L}{di} = -\kappa\). With \(\kappa = 15\), one percentage point more interest (0.01) lowers money demand by about 15% (exactly 13.9%).
FormulaGeometric series and present value

Geometric series (geometrische Reihe)

\[ 1 + x + x^2 + \dots + x^n = \frac{1 - x^{n+1}}{1 - x} \quad (x \neq 1) \] \[ 1 + x + x^2 + \dots = \frac{1}{1 - x} \quad (|x| < 1) \]

Keynesian multiplier (Multiplikator)

\[ \Delta Y = \left(1 + c_1 + c_1^2 + \dots\right)\Delta G = \frac{1}{1 - c_1}\,\Delta G \]

Compound interest and present value (Zinseszins, Barwert)

\[ K_n = K_0\,(1+i)^n \qquad V = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{z}{(1+i)^t} \] \[ \text{Perpetuity (ewige Rente): } V = \frac{z}{i} \]

\(c_1\) is the marginal propensity to consume (marginale Konsumquote). A present value is a geometric series with \(x = 1/(1+i)\).

GraphThe multiplier as a geometric series

Extra government spending \(\Delta G = 1\) becomes someone's income. They spend the share \(c_1\) of it, which becomes someone else's income, and so on. The rounds add up to the multiplier.

Multiplier2.5

QuestionMath question 1

Simplify \(\dfrac{x^5 \cdot x^{-2}}{x^2}\) and \(\sqrt{x}\cdot x^{3/2}\).

Show answer

\(x^{5 - 2 - 2} = x\) and \(x^{1/2 + 3/2} = x^2\). Add exponents when you multiply powers of the same base, subtract them when you divide.

QuestionMath question 2

Output grows by 3% a year. How long does it take to double? Solve \(1.03^t = 2\).

Show answer

Take logs: \(t\,\ln 1.03 = \ln 2\), so \(t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.03} = \dfrac{0.6931}{0.0296} \approx 23.4\) years. The rule of 70 gives \(70/3 \approx 23.3\).

QuestionMath question 3

Solve \(x^2 - 6x + 5 = 0\).

Show answer

pq-Formel with \(p = -6\) and \(q = 5\): \(x = 3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 5} = 3 \pm 2\), so \(x_1 = 1\) and \(x_2 = 5\). Check: \(1 - 6 + 5 = 0\) and \(25 - 30 + 5 = 0\).

QuestionMath question 4

Differentiate \(f(x) = (2x + 1)^3\) and \(g(x) = x^2 \ln x\).

Show answer

Chain rule: \(f'(x) = 3(2x+1)^2 \cdot 2 = 6(2x+1)^2\).

Product rule: \(g'(x) = 2x \ln x + x^2 \cdot \frac{1}{x} = x\,(2\ln x + 1)\).

QuestionMath question 5

A firm's profit is \(G(x) = -x^2 + 12x - 20\). Which quantity maximizes profit, and how high is the profit?

Show answer

\(G'(x) = -2x + 12 = 0\) gives \(x^* = 6\). \(G''(x) = -2 < 0\), so it is a maximum. \(G(6) = -36 + 72 - 20 = 16\).

QuestionMath question 6

\(Y = K^{0.3}N^{0.7}\). Capital grows by 10% and labor by 2%. By about how much does output grow?

Show answer

\(g_Y \approx 0.3 \cdot 10\% + 0.7 \cdot 2\% = 4.4\%\). The exact value is \(1.1^{0.3} \cdot 1.02^{0.7} - 1 = 4.3\%\). The approximation is a little high because 10% is not that small.

QuestionMath question 7

The nominal interest rate is 5% and expected inflation is 2%. What is the real interest rate, exactly and approximately?

Show answer

Exactly \(r = \frac{1.05}{1.02} - 1 = 2.94\%\). Approximately \(r \approx i - \pi^e = 3\%\).

QuestionMath question 8

The marginal propensity to consume is \(c_1 = 0.75\). Government spending rises by €20 bn. By how much does output rise in the end?

Show answer

The multiplier is \(\frac{1}{1 - 0.75} = 4\), so \(\Delta Y = 4 \times 20 = 80\): output rises by €80 bn. Set \(c_1 = 0.75\) in the 0.6 graph to see the rounds.

QuestionMath question 9

Demand is \(x = 100 - 2p\). What is the price elasticity of demand at \(p = 20\)? Is demand elastic or inelastic there?

Show answer

\(x = 60\) and \(\frac{dx}{dp} = -2\), so \(\varepsilon = -2 \cdot \frac{20}{60} = -0.67\). Since \(|\varepsilon| < 1\), demand is inelastic (unelastisch) at this price.

IdeaThinking like an economist

Microeconomics studies decisions under scarcity (Knappheit): resources are not enough to satisfy all wants, so every choice involves a trade-off. Its tools are models, optimization, and equilibrium.

  • Model (Modell): a deliberately simplified picture of reality. It keeps the essential factors and drops the rest, and it separates explaining, exogenous (exogene) variables from explained, endogenous (endogene) variables.
  • Purposeful behavior (zielgerichtetes Verhalten): the rational choice approach (homo oeconomicus) assumes people pursue clear goals. Models work "as if" people optimize, even when nobody actually calculates.
  • Equilibrium (Gleichgewicht): the outcome when individual optimal choices balance each other. It depends on the institutions (Institutionen), the "rules of the game".
  • Cost-benefit rule (Kosten-Nutzen-Vergleich): do action \(x\) if \(B(x) > C(x)\). \(B(x)\) is the most you would pay for \(x\). Costs need not be cash flows; money is just a common unit of account.
  • Reservation price (Reservationspreis): the price at which you are indifferent between doing \(x\) and not doing it.
  • Opportunity cost (Opportunitätskosten): the value of the best alternative you give up to do \(x\).
  • Sunk costs (versunkene Kosten): costs already incurred. They no longer matter for the decision.
  • Marginal cost and marginal benefit (Grenzkosten, Grenznutzen): the change in total cost or total benefit from one more unit of an activity. For "how much" decisions, expand while marginal benefit exceeds marginal cost. With a continuous activity and falling marginal benefit, choose the level where \(MB = MC\). Slide 49: at 4 cents per minute, Susanne phones 400 minutes per month.
  • Average cost and benefit (Durchschnittskosten, Durchschnittsnutzen): total divided by the number of units. They can lie above, below, or at the marginal values, so they are the wrong guide for "one more unit" decisions.
  • Positive and normative questions (positive und normative Fragestellungen): positive questions ask about effects and can be studied with theory and data (slide 52: the effects of short-time work allowance, Kurzarbeitergeld). Normative questions ask what is best and depend on values (slide 53: lockdown policy).

Slides 12 to 53. Here "Grenznutzen" means marginal benefit in money; from section 2 on it means marginal utility (MU). Cost-curve math: see 0.8.

PitfallsFour common decision errors

Slide 32 lists four typical errors in cost-benefit thinking.

  • Ignoring implicit costs: count opportunity costs. A football ticket costs 40 EUR and the match is worth 60 EUR to you, but you give up a day as a student assistant that pays 45 EUR. So \(C(x) = 40 + 45 = 85 > 60 = B(x)\): go to work (slide 35).
  • Counting sunk costs: one person won a concert ticket, another paid 40 EUR for it. With equal preferences, both should decide the same way on a stormy evening, because the 40 EUR are gone either way (slide 37). In an all-you-can-eat pizza experiment, guests whose price was refunded at random ate less: real people do let sunk costs matter (slide 38).
  • Relative instead of absolute amounts: saving 10 EUR is worth the same on a 20 EUR radio as on a 1,000 EUR TV (slide 39). A coupon cuts a Barcelona flight from 200 to 100 EUR (saves 100 EUR) or a New Delhi flight from 2,400 to 2,280 EUR (saves 120 EUR). Use it for New Delhi (slide 40).
  • Average instead of marginal values: the right question is what one more unit adds. See the fishing-boat example (slides 43 to 47).
IdeaBudget set and budget line

Consumer theory has three steps: describe what is affordable (this section), describe what the consumer likes (section 2), and pick the best affordable bundle (section 3) (slide 56).

  • Consumption bundle (Konsumbündel): \(X = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\), with prices \(p_1, \dots, p_n\) and income \(m\).
  • Budget set (Budget, Budgetmenge): all bundles whose cost does not exceed \(m\).
  • Budget line (Budgetgerade): all bundles that spend income exactly. It is the upper boundary of the budget set.
  • Slope: \(-p_1/p_2\). In absolute value it is the opportunity cost of one more unit of good 1, measured in units of good 2 at market prices.
  • Composite good (zusammengesetztes Gut): with many goods, lump "all other goods" into one good priced at 1 EUR, that is, the money spent on everything else (slide 68).
  • Shifts and rotations: an income change shifts the line in parallel and leaves opportunity costs unchanged. A change in one price rotates the line around the other intercept. A proportional change of both prices shifts it in parallel (slides 70 to 79).
  • Taxes: an ad valorem tax (Wertsteuer) at rate \(t\) on good 1 raises \(p_1\) to \((1+t)p_1\) and rotates the line. A uniform tax on all goods shifts it inward like an income cut (slides 80 to 82).
  • Vouchers (Gutscheine): with 100 EUR, prices of 1 EUR, and 40 EUR in drink tokens, food stays capped at 100 while drinks can reach 140, so the line gets a flat segment (slides 83 to 85). Reselling tokens below face value tilts that segment up toward the food axis (slide 87).
  • Quantity discount (Mengenrabatt): the line kinks where the price changes (slides 88 to 93).
  • Numéraire (Numéraire): a line needs only two numbers but the budget has three prices (\(p_1\), \(p_2\), \(m\)), so one can be set to 1. Only relative prices matter (slides 94 to 95).
  • Further constraints: a minimum amount of food or a time budget cut the set further. The feasible set is the intersection of all constraints (slides 96 to 100).

Record example (slides 57, 58, 101): losing a 10 EUR note and breaking a 10 EUR record both shift the budget line in by 10 EUR, so the decision whether to buy the record (again) should be the same.

FormulaBudget line formulas

Budget set, n goods (Budgetmenge)

\[ p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 + \dots + p_nx_n \le m \]

Budget line, two goods (Budgetgerade)

\[ p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 = m \] \[ x_2 = \frac{m}{p_2} - \frac{p_1}{p_2}\,x_1 \]

Intercepts and slope (Achsenabschnitte, Steigung)

\[ x_1\text{-axis: } \frac{m}{p_1},\qquad x_2\text{-axis: } \frac{m}{p_2} \] \[ \frac{\Delta x_2}{\Delta x_1} = -\frac{p_1}{p_2} \]

One more unit of good 1 costs \(p_1/p_2\) units of good 2; one more unit of good 2 costs \(p_2/p_1\) units of good 1 (slide 66).

Uniform ad valorem tax (einheitliche Wertsteuer)

\[ (1+t)p_1x_1 + (1+t)p_2x_2 = m \] \[ p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 = \frac{m}{1+t} \]

Numéraire: divide by \(p_1\) (slides 94 to 95)

\[ 2x_1 + 3x_2 = 12 \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 + \tfrac{3}{2}x_2 = 6 \]

Decision rules (Entscheidungsregeln)

\[ \text{do } x \text{ if } B(x) > C(x) \] \[ \text{choose } x^* \text{ with } MB(x^*) = MC(x^*) \]

Tax note: the uniform tax works like an income tax rate \(\tau\) with \(1 - \tau = \frac{1}{1+t}\), so \(\tau = \frac{t}{1+t}\). Slide 80 prints \(\frac{1}{t+1}\); that is the share of income left after tax, not the tax rate.

ExampleShould Tom add a fourth boat?

Tom runs 3 fishing boats. Daily costs are 300 EUR, daily revenue is 600 EUR (slide 43). He argues: revenue per boat (200 EUR) exceeds cost per boat (100 EUR), so he should add a boat. Each boat adds 100 EUR of cost: that is the marginal cost (slide 45).

BoatsTotal / marginal / average benefit (EUR per day)
1300 / 300 / 300
2480 / 180 / 240
3600 / 120 / 200
4640 / 40 / 160
  1. Compare at the margin: boats 1 to 3 each add more than 100 EUR (300, 180, and 120 EUR).
  2. The fourth boat adds only 40 EUR of revenue but costs 100 EUR.
  3. Result: keep 3 boats. Profit would fall from \(600 - 300 = 300\) EUR to \(640 - 400 = 240\) EUR with a fourth boat.

At 4 boats the average benefit (160 EUR) still exceeds the cost per boat (100 EUR). That is why averages mislead. Slides 43 to 47.

Macro linkMargins and budgets in macro
  • Models and variables: macro textbooks start with the same method. A model links endogenous to exogenous variables, and comparative statics asks what changes when an exogenous variable moves.
  • Intertemporal budget constraint (intertemporale Budgetbeschränkung): in the two-period consumption model (Fisher model), the budget line links consumption today and tomorrow. Its slope, \(-(1+r)\), is the opportunity cost of consuming today.
  • Relative prices: if all prices and income double, the budget line does not move. Macro uses the same idea to separate real from nominal variables (real wage \(W/P\), real interest rate) and for the long-run neutrality of money in the classical model.
  • Marginal reasoning: in the classical model, firms hire labor until the marginal product of labor equals the real wage and rent capital until its marginal product equals the real rental price. Investment theory compares the marginal product of capital with its cost.
  • Opportunity cost of money: holding cash means giving up interest, so the nominal interest rate is the opportunity cost in money demand (LM curve).
QuestionMicro 1.1

Tom's fishing boats (slide 47): total daily benefit is 300, 480, 600, and 640 EUR with 1, 2, 3, and 4 boats. How many boats should he run if each boat costs 150 EUR instead of 100 EUR?

Show answer

Two boats. The marginal benefits are 300, 180, 120, and 40 EUR. The first two exceed 150 EUR, the third (120 EUR) does not. Profit check: 1 boat \(300 - 150 = 150\), 2 boats \(480 - 300 = 180\), 3 boats \(600 - 450 = 150\) EUR. Profit peaks at 2 boats.

QuestionMicro 1.2

Quantity discount (slides 88 to 93): income is 100 EUR and good 2 costs 1 EUR. Good 1 costs 2 EUR for the first 20 units and 1 EUR from the 21st unit on. Describe the budget line: slopes, kink, and intercepts.

Show answer

The line starts at \((0, 100)\) and falls with slope \(-2\) up to \(x_1 = 20\). The first 20 units cost 40 EUR, so the kink is at \((20, 60)\). After that the slope is \(-1\): the remaining 60 EUR buy 60 more units of good 1, so the line reaches the \(x_1\) axis at 80. Without the discount it would end at \(100/2 = 50\).

IdeaPreferences and indifference curves

Section 1 described what a consumer can afford. Preferences (Präferenzen) describe what she likes (slide 104).

  • Preference relations (Präferenzrelationen): \(x \succ y\) is strict preference (strenge Bevorzugung), \(x \sim y\) indifference (Indifferenz), \(x \succeq y\) weak preference (schwache Bevorzugung). \(x \succeq y\) and \(y \succeq x\) together mean \(x \sim y\). The relations rank bundles but say nothing about how much better one is: they are ordinal (slides 105 to 106).
  • Completeness (Vollständigkeit): any two bundles can be compared. Taken literally it almost never holds; its purpose is to rule out a consumer who cannot choose at all (slide 108).
  • Transitivity (Transitivität): if \(x \succeq y\) and \(y \succeq z\), then \(x \succeq z\). With cyclic preferences, a "money pump" could take all your money through repeated trades with a small fee (slides 109 to 110).
  • Indifference curve (Indifferenzkurve): all bundles exactly as good as a reference bundle. The weakly preferred set (WP) includes the curve, the strictly preferred set (SP) does not (slides 113 to 115).
  • No crossing: indifference curves cannot cross. If they did, transitivity would make two bundles indifferent that the curves rank differently (slide 116).
  • Goods and bads (Gut, Ungut): more of a good is better, less of a bad is better. Two goods or two bads: negative slope. One good and one bad (horsepower and exhaust): positive slope (slides 117 to 119).
  • Satiation (Sättigung): there is one best bundle, the satiation point (Sättigungspunkt). Non-satiation (Nichtsättigung) means more is always preferred (slides 120 to 121).
  • Monotonicity (Monotonie): more is better, other things equal, or at least not worse. Justified by free disposal; a bad can be redefined as a good ("absence of exhaust") (slide 123).
  • Convexity (Konvexität): mixed bundles are at least as good as extremes. If (4 beers, 0 sausages) \(\sim\) (0 beers, 4 sausages), convex preferences rank (2, 2) at least as high. Strictly convex: every mix is strictly better. Weakly convex: some mixes are only equally good. Concave: mixes are worse (slides 124 to 128).
  • Extreme cases: perfect substitutes (perfekte Substitute) trade at a constant rate (red and blue pencils): straight indifference curves. Perfect complements (perfekte Komplemente) are used in fixed proportions (left and right shoes): L-shaped curves (slides 129 to 131).

Well-behaved preferences (normale Präferenzen) are monotone and convex (slide 122). Slides 104 to 131.

IdeaUtility, marginal utility, and the GRS

A utility function (Nutzenfunktion) assigns a number to every bundle so that preferred bundles get higher numbers. Economists use it to represent preferences, not to measure happiness; in practice, utility shows up in choices (slides 136 to 137).

  • Representation: complete, reflexive, transitive, and monotone preferences can be described by a continuous utility function (slide 137).
  • Ordinal utility (ordinaler Nutzen): only the ranking counts. \(U(x) = 6\) and \(U(y) = 2\) means \(x \succ y\), not that \(x\) is three times as good (slide 138). All bundles on one indifference curve share one utility level (slide 139).
  • Monotone transformation (monotone Transformation): any order-preserving \(f\), such as \(U^2\), \(2U + 10\), or \(\ln U\), represents the same preferences and leaves the GRS unchanged (slides 146 to 150, 186 to 189; proof in 0.7).
  • Marginal rate of substitution (Grenzrate der Substitution, GRS): how much of good 2 a person will give up for one more unit of good 1; the slope of the indifference curve at that point. The slides define \(GRS = dx_2/dx_1\), so it is negative for two goods (slides 132 to 133).
  • Diminishing GRS (abnehmende GRS): with strictly convex preferences, the GRS rises toward zero as \(x_1\) grows. Slide 134 shows \(-5\) where \(x_1\) is small and \(-0.5\) where \(x_1\) is large.
  • Marginal utility (Grenznutzen, MU): the change in utility from a small increase in one good, all other goods held constant (slides 172 to 175).
  • GRS from marginal utilities: along an indifference curve utility stays constant, so \(GRS = -MU_1/MU_2\) (slides 176 to 179; derivation from \(dU = 0\) in 0.7).
  • Standard utility functions: perfect substitutes, perfect complements, quasi-linear (quasi-linear), and Cobb-Douglas (see the card "Utility function types"). Quasi-linear indifference curves are vertical shifts of one curve and have the same slope at a given \(x_1\). Cobb-Douglas curves approach both axes but never touch them (slides 151 to 171, 183 to 185).
FormulaPreferences and utility in symbols

Relations (Präferenzrelationen)

\[ x \succ y,\qquad x \sim y,\qquad x \succeq y \]

Transitivity (Transitivität)

\[ x \succeq y \text{ and } y \succeq z \;\Rightarrow\; x \succeq z \]

Convex mix, \(0 < t < 1\) (slide 125)

\[ z = \big(tx_1 + (1-t)y_1,\; tx_2 + (1-t)y_2\big) \]

Utility represents preferences (slide 137)

\[ x \succ y \iff U(x) > U(y) \] \[ x \sim y \iff U(x) = U(y) \]

Marginal utility (Grenznutzen)

\[ MU_1 = \frac{\partial U(x_1,x_2)}{\partial x_1} \] \[ MU_2 = \frac{\partial U(x_1,x_2)}{\partial x_2} \]

Marginal rate of substitution (GRS)

\[ GRS = \frac{dx_2}{dx_1} = -\frac{MU_1}{MU_2} \]

Sign convention: the slides keep the minus sign, so the GRS of two goods is negative and "diminishing" refers to its absolute value. Derivation of \(GRS = -MU_1/MU_2\) and why monotone transformations leave the GRS unchanged: see 0.7.

FormulaUtility function types
PreferencesUtility function and GRS
Perfect substitutes (perfekte Substitute)\(U = ax_1 + bx_2\), \(GRS = -a/b\), constant. Pencils: \(U = x_1 + x_2\), \(GRS = -1\).
Perfect complements (perfekte Komplemente)\(U = \min\{ax_1, bx_2\}\), kink on the ray \(ax_1 = bx_2\). GRS is not defined at the kink, \(-\infty\) on the vertical leg, 0 on the horizontal leg. Shoes: \(\min\{x_1, x_2\}\). One flashlight, two batteries: \(\min\{x_1, x_2/2\}\).
Quasi-linear (quasi-linear)\(U = f(x_1) + x_2\), \(GRS = -f'(x_1)\). Indifference curves: \(x_2 = k - f(x_1)\) with \(k = \bar U\).
Cobb-Douglas\(U = x_1^c x_2^d\) with \(c, d > 0\), \(GRS = -\dfrac{c\,x_2}{d\,x_1}\).

Slides 151 to 171, 183, and 223. Equivalent Cobb-Douglas forms (log form, exponents summing to 1, slides 170 to 171): see 0.7. How these shapes lead to interior, corner, and kink choices: section 3 and 0.7.

ExampleU = x1 x2: ranking and GRS

Slides 139 to 149 and 180 to 182 use one utility function, \(U(x_1,x_2) = x_1x_2\).

  1. Rank three bundles: \(U(2,3) = 6\), \(U(4,1) = 4\), \(U(2,2) = 4\). So \((2,3) \succ (4,1) \sim (2,2)\).
  2. Transform: \(V = U^2\) gives 36, 16, and 16; \(W = 2U + 10\) gives 22, 18, and 18. The ranking is the same, so all three functions describe the same preferences (slides 148 to 149).
  3. Marginal utilities: \(MU_1 = x_2\) and \(MU_2 = x_1\), so \(GRS = -x_2/x_1\).
  4. Evaluate: \(GRS(1,8) = -8\). With little of good 1, she gives up about 8 units of good 2 for one more unit of good 1. \(GRS(6,6) = -1\): she trades one for one.
  5. Check the transformation: for \(V = x_1^2x_2^2\), \(GRS = -\frac{2x_1x_2^2}{2x_1^2x_2} = -\frac{x_2}{x_1}\), unchanged (slide 189).
Macro linkPreferences in macro models
  • Preferences over time: the two-period consumption model (Fisher model) draws indifference curves over consumption today and tomorrow, with the same axioms: more is better and curves do not cross.
  • Convexity and consumption smoothing: convex preferences favor mixed bundles over extremes. Over time this means households prefer smooth consumption to feast and famine, the core idea of the permanent income and life-cycle hypotheses.
  • Diminishing marginal utility: macro models usually assume that the marginal utility of consumption is positive but falling. An extra euro of consumption is worth more in bad times than in good times.
  • Consumption and leisure: models with labor supply give households utility from consumption and leisure. The trade-off between the two is drawn with the same indifference curves.
  • Cobb-Douglas and logs: the Cobb-Douglas form returns as the production function \(Y = K^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}\) (Solow model). Taking logs, as on slide 170, turns the product into a sum; growth accounting builds on this.
QuestionMicro 2.1

Left and right shoes are perfect complements (slide 131). Rank the bundles (5, 5), (5, 9), (9, 5), and (9, 9). Which utility function represents these preferences?

Show answer

\(U(x_1, x_2) = \min\{x_1, x_2\}\), the number of pairs. (5, 5), (5, 9), and (9, 5) each give 5 pairs, so \(U = 5\) and the three bundles are indifferent: extra shoes of one kind add nothing. (9, 9) gives 9 pairs, \(U = 9\), so it is strictly preferred to the other three.

QuestionMicro 2.2

Slide 175 uses \(U = x_1^{1/2}x_2^{2}\). Compute \(MU_1\), \(MU_2\), and the GRS.

Show answer

\(MU_1 = \frac{1}{2}x_1^{-1/2}x_2^{2}\) and \(MU_2 = 2x_1^{1/2}x_2\) (slide 175). Then \(GRS = -\frac{MU_1}{MU_2} = -\frac{\frac{1}{2}x_1^{-1/2}x_2^{2}}{2x_1^{1/2}x_2} = -\frac{x_2}{4x_1}\). This matches the Cobb-Douglas rule \(GRS = -\frac{c\,x_2}{d\,x_1}\) with \(c = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(d = 2\).

IdeaThe best affordable bundle

Optimal choice (optimale Entscheidung) means picking the best bundle the budget allows: the point on the highest reachable indifference curve (slide 191).

  • Interior solution (innere Lösung, Tangentiallösung): the indifference curve just touches the budget line. Both slopes are equal: \(GRS = -p_1/p_2\) (slides 194, 196, 200).
  • Equal marginal utility per euro: equivalently \(MU_1/p_1 = MU_2/p_2\). The last euro spent on each good yields the same extra utility (slide 196).
  • Why it must hold: if the consumer's willingness to trade (GRS) differs from the market's exchange rate (price ratio), trading at market prices reaches a higher indifference curve. She keeps trading until both match (slides 195 to 196).
  • Corner solution (Randlösung): the optimum lies on an axis and one good is not bought. She would like to keep trading, but has no units of that good left to give up. With \(x_1 = 0\): \(|GRS| < p_1/p_2\) (slides 198 to 200).
  • Information in prices (Informationsgehalt von Preisen): everyone faces the same price ratio, so in the optimum everyone has the same GRS, whatever their preferences. Prices therefore summarize how all buyers value goods relative to each other and signal producers what to make (slide 197).
  • Demand (Nachfrage): the best affordable bundle at given prices and income, written \(x_1^*(p_1, p_2, m)\) and \(x_2^*(p_1, p_2, m)\) (slide 201).
  • Lagrange method (Lagrange-Verfahren): maximize \(U\) subject to the budget. The first-order conditions give the tangency condition plus the budget line (slides 211 to 215; worked example in 0.7).

Sign convention: slides 194 and 196 write \(GRS = P_1/P_2\) in absolute values, slide 200 writes \(GRS = -P_1/P_2\). Both state the same tangency condition.

IdeaSpecial preferences and in-kind transfers
  • Cobb-Douglas: always an interior optimum. The exponents fix the spending shares: good 1 gets the share \(a/(a+b)\) of income, whatever the prices (slides 217 to 218).
  • Perfect substitutes: with \(U = x_1 + x_2\), the consumer buys only the cheaper good, a corner solution. If \(p_1 = p_2\), every bundle on the budget line is optimal (slides 219 to 221).
  • Concave preferences: the tangency point is the worst bundle on the budget line. The optimum is a corner (slide 222).
  • Perfect complements: the optimum sits at the kink on the ray \(x_2 = ax_1\), where the GRS is not defined. Instead of a tangency condition, combine the ray with the budget line (slides 223 to 225).
  • Cash transfer vs housing subsidy (Geldtransfer vs Wohnkostenzuschuss): a subsidy can only pay rent, so it cuts off part of the budget line that an equal cash transfer would allow. If the household would spend at least the subsidy amount on rent anyway, both instruments lead to the same bundle. If it would spend less, the subsidy forces higher rent and a lower utility level. The state still uses in-kind help because it wants to support housing, not other goods (slides 202 to 209).
  • Household production (Haushaltsproduktion): preferences can also be defined over "commodities" that households produce from market goods with a consumption technology or household production function. This explains, for example, why demand for a wool sweater differs between winter and summer without assuming that preferences change. The approach is plausible but cumbersome, so the course uses it only as a thinking tool (slide 210).

Corner and kink solutions with formulas, plus the interactive optimal-choice graph: see 0.7.

FormulaOptimality conditions

Tangency (Marginalbedingung, inneres Optimum)

\[ GRS = -\frac{MU_1}{MU_2} = -\frac{p_1}{p_2} \]

Equal marginal utility per euro

\[ \frac{MU_1}{p_1} = \frac{MU_2}{p_2} \]

Budget is fully spent

\[ p_1x_1^* + p_2x_2^* = m \]

Corner solution with \(x_1^* = 0\) (Randlösung, slide 200)

\[ |GRS| < \frac{p_1}{p_2} \;\Leftrightarrow\; \frac{MU_1}{p_1} < \frac{MU_2}{p_2} \]

Demand functions (Nachfragefunktionen)

\[ x_1^*(p_1, p_2, m),\qquad x_2^*(p_1, p_2, m) \]

Two equations, two unknowns: the tangency condition and the budget line pin down \(x_1^*\) and \(x_2^*\). Slides 194 to 201 and 211 to 212. The Lagrange route, the Cobb-Douglas demand \(x_1^* = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_1}\) (slide 218), and the demand for perfect substitutes and complements (slides 219 to 225): see 0.7.

ExampleFinding the best bundle on slide 194

Income \(m = 100\), prices \(p_1 = 5\) and \(p_2 = 10\). The budget line \(5x_1 + 10x_2 = 100\) runs from 20 units of good 1 to 10 units of good 2, with slope \(-1/2\) (slides 192 to 194).

BundleCost \(5x_1 + 10x_2\) and verdict
D (6, 5)\(30 + 50 = 80\): affordable, but money is left. By monotonicity it cannot be best.
A (2, 9)\(10 + 90 = 100\): on the budget line, but on the same curve \(I_1\) as D.
E (16, 2)\(80 + 20 = 100\): on the budget line, also on \(I_1\). By transitivity, A and E are no better than D.
G (15, 8)\(75 + 80 = 155\): on the highest curve \(I_3\), but not affordable.
F (8, 6)\(40 + 60 = 100\): on the budget line and on \(I_2\), the highest reachable curve. This is the optimum.

At F the indifference curve touches the budget line once, so \(|GRS| = p_1/p_2 = 5/10 = 0.5\).

Macro linkOptimal choice in macro
  • Optimal consumption over time: in the two-period model (Fisher model), the household picks the point where its indifference curve over consumption today and tomorrow touches the intertemporal budget line, so the GRS equals \(1 + r\) in absolute value. Saving is current income minus current consumption.
  • Borrowing constraints: if the household cannot borrow, the budget set is cut at current income, like the extra constraints in section 1. The optimum can then be a corner where consumption equals current income.
  • Euler equation: "equal marginal utility per euro" across periods becomes the consumption Euler equation: marginal utility today equals the discounted, interest-adjusted marginal utility tomorrow. It underlies the random-walk hypothesis of consumption and the dynamic IS curve of New Keynesian models.
  • Constant shares: Cobb-Douglas consumers spend fixed income shares. With a Cobb-Douglas production function and competitive factor markets, capital and labor likewise receive constant shares \(\alpha\) and \(1 - \alpha\) of national income.
  • Prices as signals: in the classical loanable funds market, the real interest rate brings saving and investment into balance, just as relative prices coordinate consumers here.
QuestionMicro 3.1

Slides 192 to 195: income is 100, \(p_1 = 5\), \(p_2 = 10\). At the affordable bundle A = (2, 9), the GRS is 1 in absolute value. Why does the consumer gain by buying less of good 2 and more of good 1?

Show answer

At A she would give up 1 unit of good 2 for 1 more unit of good 1 and stay equally well off. The market asks less: \(p_1/p_2 = 0.5\). Giving up 1 unit of good 2 frees \(p_2 = 10\) of income, which buys 2 units of good 1, one more than she needs to stay indifferent. So she reaches a higher indifference curve. She keeps trading until \(|GRS| = 0.5\), which happens at F = (8, 6), where \(5 \cdot 8 + 10 \cdot 6 = 100\).

QuestionMicro 3.2

Slides 202 to 208: a household has 500 EUR per week. The state gives either 290 EUR in cash or a 290 EUR housing subsidy that can only pay rent. When do both lead to the same choice, and when is the household worse off with the subsidy?

Show answer

Cash shifts the budget line out in parallel, to 790 EUR on both axes. The subsidy gives the same line, except that other consumption cannot exceed 500 EUR: the line runs flat from F (no rent, 500 EUR other consumption) to the kink D (290 EUR rent, 500 EUR other consumption), then down along the cash line. If with cash the household would spend more than 290 EUR on rent, its optimum lies on the shared part of the line, so the choice is identical. If it would spend less than 290 EUR on rent, that point is not reachable with the subsidy. The household ends at the kink D, spends more on rent than it wants, and reaches a lower indifference curve. The subsidy is never better than cash for the household.

IdeaFrom optimal choice to demand curves

A demand function (Nachfragefunktion) tells you how much of a good the consumer buys at given prices and income. It comes straight from the optimal choice: change one price, keep everything else fixed, and record the new optimum each time. This is comparative statics (komparative Statik).

  • Price-consumption curve (Preis-Konsumkurve): lower \(p_1\) with \(p_2\) and \(m\) fixed. The budget line pivots around its \(x_2\) intercept and gets flatter. The line through all optimal bundles is the price-consumption curve.
  • Demand curve (Nachfragekurve): plot each optimal \(x_1^*\) against the \(p_1\) that produced it, with \(p_1\) on the vertical axis. Same information as the price-consumption curve, different diagram (slides 229 to 237).
  • Cobb-Douglas case: spending on each good is a fixed share of income. So \(x_2^*\) does not move when \(p_1\) changes: the price-consumption curve is horizontal, and the demand curve for good 1 is a hyperbola (slides 238 to 240).
  • Ordinary good (gewöhnliches Gut): demand always rises when its own price falls.
  • Giffen good (Giffen-Gut): in some price range, demand falls when its own price falls, so the demand curve slopes upward there (slides 257 to 258). Section 5 explains how this can happen.
  • Cross-price effect (Kreuzpreiseffekt): how \(x_1\) reacts to \(p_2\). Good 1 is a substitute (Substitut) for good 2 if a higher \(p_2\) raises \(x_1\), and a complement (Komplement) if it lowers \(x_1\). Perfect complements are complements in this sense. With Cobb-Douglas, \(x_1^*\) does not depend on \(p_2\), so the goods are neither (slides 259 to 261).

Deriving demand functions (Lagrange, corner solutions, kinks): see 0.7. Slides 226 to 261.

IdeaIncome changes: Engel curves and preference types

Now fix both prices and raise income \(m\). The budget line shifts out in parallel (slides 262 to 266).

  • Income-consumption curve (Einkommens-Konsumkurve): the line through the optimal bundles for different incomes.
  • Engel curve (Engelkurve): income \(m\) on the vertical axis, the optimal \(x_1^*\) on the horizontal axis. One Engel curve per good.
  • Normal good (normales Gut): demand rises with income, so the Engel curve slopes upward (slide 269: tenderloin).
  • Inferior good (inferiores Gut): demand falls as income rises, so the Engel curve has a negative slope (slide 269: hamburger). Typical for low-quality goods (slide 267).
  • Luxury good (Luxusgut) and necessity (notwendiges Gut): demand for a luxury grows faster than income in percentage terms. Demand for a necessity grows slower (slide 271).
  • Homothetic preferences (homothetische Präferenzen): only the ratio of the two goods matters, not the scale. Income-consumption curve and Engel curves are rays through the origin: multiply income by \(k\) and demand multiplies by \(k\). Rare in reality, useful for illustration (slides 270 to 271).
  • Quasi-linear preferences (quasi-lineare Präferenzen): \(U = f(x_1) + x_2\). Above a threshold income, every extra euro goes to good 2 and \(x_1\) stays at \(\tilde x_1\). The Engel curve for good 1 turns vertical, so these preferences are not homothetic (slides 272 to 275).
  • Market demand (Marktnachfrage): add the individual demand curves horizontally, that is, add quantities at each price (see 0.10). With nonlinear Engel curves, the income distribution matters, not just average income (slides 276 to 286).
FormulaDemand functions for the standard cases

Cobb-Douglas \(U = x_1^a x_2^b\) (slide 238)

\[ x_1^* = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_1} \] \[ x_2^* = \frac{b}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_2} \]

Perfect complements \(U = \min\{x_1, x_2\}\) (slide 244)

\[ x_1^* = x_2^* = \frac{m}{p_1 + p_2} \]

Perfect substitutes \(U = x_1 + x_2\) (slides 250 to 256)

\[ p_1 < p_2: \; x_1^* = \tfrac{m}{p_1}, \; x_2^* = 0 \] \[ p_1 > p_2: \; x_1^* = 0, \; x_2^* = \tfrac{m}{p_2} \] \[ p_1 = p_2: \; \text{any } 0 \le x_1^* \le \tfrac{m}{p_1} \]

Quasi-linear \(U = \ln x_1 + x_2\) (slides 273 to 274)

\[ m > p_2: \; x_1^* = \frac{p_2}{p_1}, \; x_2^* = \frac{m}{p_2} - 1 \] \[ m \le p_2: \; x_1^* = \frac{m}{p_1}, \; x_2^* = 0 \]

In the interior quasi-linear case, \(x_1^*\) does not depend on \(m\). All four demand functions fall in their own price, so all are ordinary goods. Derivations: see 0.7.

FormulaClassifying goods by how demand reacts
TermTest
Ordinary good (gewöhnliches Gut)\(x_1\) rises whenever \(p_1\) falls
Giffen good (Giffen-Gut)\(x_1\) falls when \(p_1\) falls, in some range
Substitute (Substitut)\(\Delta x_1/\Delta p_2 > 0\)
Complement (Komplement)\(\Delta x_1/\Delta p_2 < 0\)
Normal good (normales Gut)\(\Delta x_1/\Delta m > 0\)
Inferior good (inferiores Gut)\(\Delta x_1/\Delta m < 0\)
Luxury good (Luxusgut)\(x_1\) grows by a larger percentage than \(m\)
Necessity (notwendiges Gut)\(x_1\) grows by a smaller percentage than \(m\)

Homothetic preferences, for all \(k > 0\) (slide 270)

\[ (x_1,x_2) \prec (y_1,y_2) \] \[ \Leftrightarrow\; (kx_1,kx_2) \prec (ky_1,ky_2) \]

Cross-price effects of the slide examples (slides 260 to 261)

\[ \text{Complements: } \frac{\partial x_1^*}{\partial p_2} = -\frac{m}{(p_1+p_2)^2} < 0 \] \[ \text{Cobb-Douglas: } \frac{\partial}{\partial p_2}\Big(\frac{am}{(a+b)p_1}\Big) = 0 \]

Slide 259 defines substitutes and complements with \(\Delta x_1/\Delta p_2\); slides 260 to 261 use the derivative. Slides 257 to 271.

ExampleDavid's demand for good 1

David has \(U(x_1,x_2) = 10\,x_1^{1/4}x_2^{3/4}\), income \(m = 100\), and \(p_2 = 2\). Find his demand function for good 1 (slide 241).

  1. Lagrange function (slide 242): \(L = 10x_1^{1/4}x_2^{3/4} - \lambda(p_1x_1 + 2x_2 - 100)\).
  2. Solve the first two conditions for \(\lambda\) and set them equal (slide 243): \[ \frac{5}{2p_1}\Big(\frac{x_2}{x_1}\Big)^{3/4} = \frac{15}{4}\Big(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\Big)^{1/4} \] This gives \(x_1 = \frac{2}{3p_1}x_2\), so \(3p_1x_1 = 2x_2\): David spends three times as much on good 2 as on good 1.
  3. Insert into the budget \(p_1x_1 + 2x_2 = 100\): \(p_1x_1 + 3p_1x_1 = 100\), so \[ x_1^* = \frac{25}{p_1} \]
  4. Shortcut check with the Cobb-Douglas formula: \(a = 1/4\), \(b = 3/4\), so \(x_1^* = \frac{1}{4}\cdot\frac{100}{p_1}\). The factor 10 is a monotone transformation and changes nothing (see 0.7).

Reading the result: David always spends 25 on good 1, a quarter of his income. At \(p_1 = 1\) he buys 25 units, at \(p_1 = 5\) only 5. His demand for good 2 is \(x_2^* = 75/2 = 37.5\) at every \(p_1\), so his price-consumption curve is horizontal.

Slides 241 to 243. The last paragraph is an own calculation from the same formulas.

Macro linkDemand in Makroökonomik
  • Aggregate demand is not market demand: the aggregate demand curve (gesamtwirtschaftliche Nachfragekurve) of the AD-AS model is not a horizontal sum of individual demand curves. It slopes down because a higher price level lowers real money balances, which raises the interest rate and reduces spending (IS-LM).
  • Consumption function: the Keynesian consumption function \(C = c_0 + c_1(Y - T)\) with \(0 < c_1 < 1\) works like an aggregate Engel curve. It shows how spending reacts to income at given prices, and treats consumption as a normal good.
  • Distribution matters: slides 282 to 286 show that redistribution changes market demand when Engel curves are nonlinear. In macro, the same point appears when households have different marginal propensities to consume (marginale Konsumneigung): shifting income toward high-propensity households raises aggregate consumption.
  • Substitutes across borders: domestic and foreign goods are substitutes. A real depreciation makes domestic goods relatively cheaper, so export quantities rise and import quantities fall. Whether net exports rise in value depends on the Marshall-Lerner condition.
QuestionMicro 4.1

Quasi-linear utility \(U = \ln x_1 + x_2\), prices \(p_1 = 1\) and \(p_2 = 2\). Find the optimal bundle for \(m = 1\), \(m = 10\), and \(m = 20\). What does the Engel curve for good 1 look like?

Show answer

The interior formulas \(x_1^* = p_2/p_1\) and \(x_2^* = m/p_2 - 1\) hold only if \(m > p_2 = 2\) (slides 273 to 274).

\(m = 10\): \(x_1^* = 2\), \(x_2^* = 10/2 - 1 = 4\). Check: \(1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 4 = 10\).

\(m = 20\): \(x_1^* = 2\), \(x_2^* = 9\). Check: \(2 + 18 = 20\). All extra income goes to good 2.

\(m = 1 \le p_2\): corner solution, \(x_2^* = 0\) and \(x_1^* = m/p_1 = 1\).

Engel curve for good 1: \(x_1^* = m/p_1\) rises until \(m = p_2 = 2\), where \(x_1^* = \tilde x_1 = 2\). Above that it is vertical. Not a ray through the origin, so not homothetic (slide 275).

QuestionMicro 4.2

A and B have identical preferences and each earn 120 euros per week. Their Engel curve for food gives 10 units at 120 euros, 6 units at 60 euros, and 12 units at 180 euros. A's income falls by 50 percent, B's rises by 50 percent. What happens to average income and to total food demand, and why?

Show answer

New incomes are 60 and 180 euros, so average income stays at 120 euros.

Food demand before: \(10 + 10 = 20\). After: \(6 + 12 = 18\). Total demand falls by 2 (slide 284).

Reason: the Engel curve is not linear. Losing 60 euros cuts A's food demand by 4, while gaining 60 euros raises B's only by 2. So average income is not enough to predict market demand: the distribution matters (slides 282 to 286). Redistribution from rich to poor tends to raise demand for food and lower demand for luxuries (slide 286).

IdeaSplitting a price change into two effects

A price change does two things at once (slides 289 to 291). It changes relative prices: the good becomes more or less attractive than its substitutes. And it changes purchasing power (Kaufkraft): with the same money income, the consumer can buy more or less than before.

  • Substitution effect (Substitutionseffekt): the part of the total change caused by the new relative prices alone.
  • Income effect (Einkommenseffekt): the part caused by the change in purchasing power alone.
  • Total effect (Gesamteffekt): substitution effect plus income effect.
  • Slutsky compensation: after \(p_1\) falls, reduce income to \(m^{\text{const}}\), just enough to buy the old bundle \((x_1', x_2')\) at the new prices. Graphically: a budget line with the new slope through the old bundle. Its optimum \((x_1'', x_2'')\) gives the substitution effect (slides 292 to 298).
  • Income effect step: give the income back, from \(m^{\text{const}}\) to \(m\), at the new price. The budget line shifts out in parallel to the final optimum \((x_1''', x_2''')\) (slides 299 to 303).
  • Hicks substitution effect (Hicks-Substitutionseffekt): holds utility constant instead of purchasing power. The budget line with the new slope is rolled along the original indifference curve; the tangency point gives the substitution effect (slides 307 to 308).

Slutsky asks: can you still afford what you bought before? Hicks asks: are you still as well off as before? For small price changes, both give almost the same answer.

IdeaSign rules and Giffen goods

The rules hold for the usual convex indifference curves (slide 304).

CaseEffect on \(x_1\) when \(p_1\) rises
Substitution effect (Slutsky or Hicks)Always negative: opposite to the price change
Income effect, normal goodNegative: reinforces the substitution effect. Total effect negative.
Income effect, inferior goodPositive: works against the substitution effect. Total effect ambiguous.
Giffen goodInferior, and the income effect outweighs the substitution effect. Total effect positive.
Quasi-linear, interior solutionIncome effect zero. Total effect equals substitution effect.
  • Giffen conditions (slide 305): a Giffen good must be inferior. It must also take a large share of the budget, so the income effect is big, and have a small substitution effect.
  • Do Giffen goods exist? (slide 306): very unlikely. Most goods take a small budget share. Define a good more broadly to raise its share, and it is less likely to be inferior. Inferior goods tend to have close substitutes. Candidates: potatoes historically, and leisure in the consumption-leisure choice.
  • Salt versus shelter (slides 309 to 316): salt has no close substitute (almost L-shaped indifference curves) and a tiny budget share. With 1 kg per month at 0.30 euros and an income of 1,200 euros, the share is 0.00025; doubling the price only lifts it to 0.0005. Both effects are negligible. Shelter takes a large share and has substitutes, so both effects are large.
FormulaSlutsky decomposition and Slutsky equation

Compensated income (slides 298 and 319)

\[ m^{\text{const}} = p_1^{\text{neu}}x_1' + p_2x_2' \] \[ \Delta m = m^{\text{const}} - m = x_1'\,\Delta p_1 \]

Substitution effect (Substitutionseffekt, slide 298)

\[ \Delta x_1^s = x_1(p_1^{\text{neu}}, m^{\text{const}}) \] \[ \qquad - x_1(p_1, m) \]

Income effect (Einkommenseffekt, slide 302)

\[ \Delta x_1^e = x_1(p_1^{\text{neu}}, m) \] \[ \qquad - x_1(p_1^{\text{neu}}, m^{\text{const}}) \]

Total effect (Gesamteffekt)

\[ \Delta x_1 = \Delta x_1^s + \Delta x_1^e \]

Slutsky demand and Slutsky equation (Slutsky-Gleichung, slide 317)

\[ x_1^s(p_1,p_2,\bar x_1,\bar x_2) \] \[ \equiv x_1(p_1,\,p_2,\,p_1\bar x_1 + p_2\bar x_2) \] \[ \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial p_1} = \frac{\partial x_1^s}{\partial p_1} - \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial m}\,\bar x_1 \]

\((\bar x_1, \bar x_2)\) is the original bundle. The income term has two parts: how demand reacts to income, and how much of good 1 the consumer bought before. The more you buy of a good, the more its price change hits your purchasing power. Slide 317 writes the substitution term as \(\partial\Delta x_1^s/\partial p_1\).

ExampleAufgabe 1: red wine gets cheaper

Demand for red wine is \(x_1(p_1, m) = \dfrac{m}{10p_1}\). Income is \(m = 800\) euros, and the price per bottle falls from 8 to 5 euros (slide 318).

  1. Old demand: \(x_1(8, 800) = 800/80 = 10\). New demand: \(x_1(5, 800) = 800/50 = 16\). Total effect: \(+6\).
  2. Income change that keeps the old bundle just affordable (slide 319): \(\Delta m = x_1\,\Delta p_1 = 10\cdot(5 - 8) = -30\), so \(m^{\text{const}} = 770\).
  3. Demand at the new price with compensated income: \(x_1(5, 770) = 770/50 = 15.4\).
  4. Substitution effect: \(\Delta x_1^s = 15.4 - 10 = 5.4\).
  5. Income effect: \(\Delta x_1^e = 16 - 15.4 = 0.6\).
  6. Check: \(5.4 + 0.6 = 6\). Both effects point the same way, so wine is a normal good here.

Slides 318 to 319. The demand \(m/(10p_1)\) is Cobb-Douglas demand with a spending share of 1/10.

PitfallsCommon mistakes with the decomposition
  • Wrong quantity in \(\Delta m\): use the old quantity, \(\Delta m = x_1'\,\Delta p_1\), not the new one.
  • Wrong order: the substitution effect compares the old optimum with the compensated optimum at the new price. The income effect compares the compensated optimum with the final optimum. Both steps use the new price.
  • Sign of the income effect: slide 302 calls it positive for normal goods because there the price falls and purchasing power rises. For a price rise it is negative for normal goods. Safer rule: for normal goods it points the same way as the substitution effect.
  • Inferior is not Giffen: being inferior is necessary for a Giffen good, not sufficient.
  • Slutsky versus Hicks: Slutsky's compensated line passes through the old bundle; Hicks's line touches the old indifference curve. The Slutsky compensated income is never lower than the Hicks one, because the old bundle is affordable and the consumer can usually do even better.
  • Quasi-linear: with an interior solution, the income effect on good 1 is zero, so the whole change is substitution (Aufgabe 2, slides 320 to 322).
Macro linkIncome and substitution effects in Makroökonomik
  • Price indices: the consumer price index (Verbraucherpreisindex) is a Laspeyres index: it prices the old basket at new prices, which is the Slutsky question. Households substitute toward goods that became relatively cheaper, so the index overstates the rise in the cost of living (substitution bias, Mankiw). A true cost-of-living index holds utility constant, like Hicks.
  • Real income: the income effect works through purchasing power. Macro measures purchasing power as real income: nominal income divided by the price level.
  • Wages and hours: a higher real wage makes leisure more expensive (substitution effect: work more) and makes the household richer (income effect: more leisure, if leisure is normal). The net effect on labor supply is ambiguous. The endowment version is in section 6.
  • Temporary versus permanent: in real business cycle theory, a temporary wage rise barely changes lifetime income, so the substitution effect dominates and people work more now (intertemporal substitution of labor). A permanent rise has a much larger income effect.
QuestionMicro 5.1

Aufgabe 2: \(U(x_1,x_2) = 4\sqrt{x_1} + x_2\), income \(m = 10\), and \(p_1 = p_2 = 1\). The price of good 1 rises to 2. Find the total effect on \(x_1\) and split it into substitution and income effect.

Show answer

Tangency: \(MU_1/MU_2 = 2/\sqrt{x_1} = p_1/p_2\), so \(x_1^* = 4(p_2/p_1)^2\) and \(x_2^* = m/p_2 - 4p_2/p_1\) (slide 321).

Old: \(x_1 = 4\), \(x_2 = 6\). New: \(x_1 = 1\), \(x_2 = 8\). Total effect: \(\Delta x_1 = -3\).

Compensated income: \(m^{\text{const}} = 10 + 4\cdot 1 = 14\). But \(x_1^*\) does not depend on \(m\), so \(x_1(2, 14) = 1\) as well.

Substitution effect \(\Delta x_1^s = -3\), income effect \(\Delta x_1^e = 0\) (slide 322).

QuestionMicro 5.2

Income is 120 euros per week. Shelter costs 0.60 euros per m², and the consumer chooses A: 100 m² plus 60 euros of other goods. The price rises to 2.40 euros per m² and she chooses D: 20 m². The budget line at the new price that just touches her old indifference curve has an intercept of 240 euros and touches it at C: 55 m². Split the total effect the Hicks way. How much income would Slutsky compensation give instead?

Show answer

Total effect: \(100 \to 20\), so \(-80\) m².

Hicks substitution effect: \(A \to C\), \(100 \to 55\), so \(-45\) m². Income effect: \(C \to D\), \(55 \to 20\), so \(-35\) m² (slides 314 to 316).

Hicks compensation: income 240, that is 120 euros extra. Slutsky compensation must make A affordable at the new price: \(2.40\cdot 100 + 60 = 300\) euros. Slutsky gives more, because with 300 euros she could buy A and still do better.

Both effects are large because shelter takes a big budget share and has substitutes.

IdeaEndowments: income from selling what you own

So far income \(m\) was given from outside (exogen). In reality, people earn income by selling what they own, such as their labor or securities (slide 325). The bundle a consumer owns before trading is the endowment (Anfangsausstattung) \(\omega = (\omega_1, \omega_2)\).

  • Income is the value of the endowment: \(m = p_1\omega_1 + p_2\omega_2\). Prices now change income too.
  • Budget line: same slope \(-p_1/p_2\) as before, but it always passes through \(\omega\). The consumer can always just keep her endowment (slides 327 to 329).
  • Gross demand (Bruttonachfrage): what the consumer ends up consuming, \(x_i\).
  • Net demand (Nettonachfrage): \(x_i - \omega_i\), what she buys or sells on the market. The value of what she buys equals the value of what she sells (slide 330).
  • Net buyer (Nettonachfrager) of good \(i\) if \(x_i > \omega_i\). Net seller (Nettoanbieter) if \(x_i < \omega_i\). With two goods, a net seller of one good is a net buyer of the other.
  • Price change: the budget line pivots around \(\omega\), not around an axis intercept (slides 334 to 336).
  • Welfare after a fall in \(p_1\) (slide 337): a net buyer of good 1 stays a buyer and is better off. A net seller who stays a seller is worse off. A seller who becomes a buyer may be better or worse off.

Why: when \(p_1\) falls, the new budget line lies above the old one to the right of \(\omega\) (where you buy good 1) and below it to the left (where you sell good 1). A buyer can still afford her old bundle. A seller who stays a seller can only pick bundles she could already afford before, and she did not choose them then.

IdeaThe endowment income effect

With an endowment, a price change has a third effect (slide 338). It also changes the value of the endowment, and so money income itself. The Slutsky decomposition now has three steps (slides 339 to 343):

  1. Pure substitution effect (reiner Substitutionseffekt): pivot the budget line through the old bundle at the new price ratio, as in section 5.
  2. Ordinary income effect (gewöhnlicher Einkommenseffekt): shift to the budget line at the new prices with the old money income \(m\).
  3. Endowment income effect (Ausstattungs-Einkommenseffekt): shift from there to the actual new budget line through \(\omega\), because the endowment is now worth a different amount.

The extended Slutsky equation (erweiterte Slutsky-Gleichung) combines both income effects into one term with the factor \(\omega_1 - \bar x_1\): the consumer's net sales of good 1 (slide 344).

  • Net buyer (\(\bar x_1 > \omega_1\)), normal good: the income term is negative, like the substitution effect. Demand falls when \(p_1\) rises.
  • Net seller (\(\bar x_1 < \omega_1\)), normal good: a higher \(p_1\) makes her richer. The income term is positive and works against the substitution effect. If it is large enough, her demand for good 1 rises with its price, even though the good is normal.

Labor supply: the slides list labor as something you sell (slide 325) and name leisure as a Giffen candidate (slide 306), but slides 324 to 344 do not build a labor supply model. Applied to time, the worker is a net seller of her time endowment: a higher wage pushes toward more work (substitution) and toward more leisure (endowment income effect).

FormulaEndowment budget and extended Slutsky equation

Budget line with endowment (slide 327)

\[ p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 = p_1\omega_1 + p_2\omega_2 \]

Net demand form (Nettonachfrage, slide 330)

\[ p_1(x_1 - \omega_1) + p_2(x_2 - \omega_2) = 0 \]

Extended Slutsky equation (erweiterte Slutsky-Gleichung, slide 344)

\[ \frac{\partial x_1}{\partial p_1} = \frac{\partial x_1^s}{\partial p_1} + (\omega_1 - \bar x_1)\frac{\partial x_1}{\partial m} \]

The same equation as three effects

\[ \text{substitution: } \frac{\partial x_1^s}{\partial p_1} < 0 \] \[ \text{ordinary income effect: } -\bar x_1\frac{\partial x_1}{\partial m} \] \[ \text{endowment income effect: } +\,\omega_1\frac{\partial x_1}{\partial m} \]

With \(\omega_1 = 0\) the last term vanishes and you are back at the Slutsky equation of section 5. The bar marks the original bundle. Slide 344 writes the substitution term as \(\partial\Delta x_1^s/\partial p_1\).

ExampleEndowment (10, 2) at prices (2, 3)

A consumer owns \(\omega = (10, 2)\): 10 units of good 1 and 2 units of good 2. Prices are \(p_1 = 2\) and \(p_2 = 3\) (slide 326).

  1. Value of the endowment, which is her income: \(2\cdot 10 + 3\cdot 2 = 26\).
  2. She chooses \((x_1^*, x_2^*) = (7, 4)\) (slide 331). It costs \(2\cdot 7 + 3\cdot 4 = 26\), so it lies on the budget line.
  3. Net form check: \(2(7 - 10) + 3(4 - 2) = -6 + 6 = 0\).
  4. Net demands: \(x_1 - \omega_1 = -3\), so she is a net seller of 3 units of good 1. \(x_2 - \omega_2 = 2\), so she is a net buyer of 2 units of good 2.
  5. In words: she sells 3 units of good 1 for a value of 6 and spends it on 2 units of good 2.

Slides 326 and 331. The cost check in step 2 and the reading in step 5 are own restatements of the slide numbers.

Macro linkEndowments in Makroökonomik
  • Two-period consumption model: the endowment is the income stream \((Y_1, Y_2)\). The budget constraint \(C_1 + \frac{C_2}{1+r} = Y_1 + \frac{Y_2}{1+r}\) passes through the endowment point with slope \(-(1+r)\) (Fisher model, as in Mankiw).
  • Savers and borrowers: a saver is a net seller of consumption today (a lender), a borrower is a net buyer. The interest rate is the relative price.
  • Higher real interest rate: for a saver, the substitution effect raises saving, but the income effect (she is now richer) lowers it, so the net effect is ambiguous. For a borrower, both effects reduce consumption today. This is the extended Slutsky sign rule.
  • Labor supply: a household's time is an endowment: it sells labor and buys consumption. A higher wage raises the value of that endowment, so the income effect favors more leisure. This is why labor supply can bend backward.
  • Terms of trade: a country that is a net exporter of a good, for example oil, gains when its price rises; a net importer loses. Same logic as slide 337.
QuestionMicro 6.1

Endowment \(\omega = (10, 2)\), prices \((2, 3)\), chosen bundle \((7, 4)\) (slide 331). Now \(p_1\) falls to 1. (a) What is the endowment worth now? (b) Can she still afford \((7, 4)\)? (c) If she stays a net seller of good 1, is she better or worse off?

Show answer

(a) \(1\cdot 10 + 3\cdot 2 = 16\).

(b) \((7, 4)\) now costs \(1\cdot 7 + 3\cdot 4 = 19 > 16\). No.

(c) Worse off (slide 337, case 1). To the left of \(\omega\), the new budget line lies below the old one. Every bundle where she still sells good 1 was affordable at the old prices, and she chose \((7, 4)\) then, so \((7, 4)\) is at least as good. Only by switching to a buyer could she possibly gain (case 2: ambiguous).

QuestionMicro 6.2

Same endowment \(\omega = (10, 2)\) and \(p_2 = 3\), but assume \(U = x_1^{1/2}x_2^{1/2}\) (own assumption, not from the slides), so \(x_1 = \frac{m}{2p_1}\) with \(m = p_1\omega_1 + p_2\omega_2\). \(p_1\) falls from 2 to 1. Split the change in \(x_1\) into substitution, ordinary income, and endowment income effect.

Show answer

Start: \(m = 26\), \(x_1 = 6.5\), \(x_2 = 26/6 = 13/3\).

Substitution: \(m^{\text{const}} = 1\cdot 6.5 + 3\cdot 13/3 = 19.5\), so \(x_1 = 19.5/2 = 9.75\). Effect \(+3.25\).

Ordinary income effect: old money income 26 at the new price gives \(x_1 = 26/2 = 13\). Effect \(+3.25\).

Endowment income effect: the endowment is now worth \(1\cdot 10 + 3\cdot 2 = 16\), so \(x_1 = 16/2 = 8\). Effect \(-5\).

Total: \(8 - 6.5 = 1.5 = 3.25 + 3.25 - 5\). She is a net seller of good 1, so the lower price makes her poorer. The discrete version of slide 344, with \(\partial x_1/\partial m = 1/2\) at the new price, gives the same income terms: \(-\bar x_1\Delta p_1\cdot\frac{1}{2} = 3.25\) and \(\omega_1\Delta p_1\cdot\frac{1}{2} = -5\).

IdeaPrice elasticity of demand

The price elasticity of demand (Preiselastizität der Nachfrage) is the percentage change in the quantity demanded when the good's own price rises by one percent. It is normally negative. Slide 347: if a 1% rise in the milk price cuts the quantity by 2%, the elasticity is \(-2\).

  • Inelastic (unelastisch), \(\varepsilon > -1\): quantity changes less than proportionally to the price.
  • Unit elastic, \(\varepsilon = -1\): quantity changes proportionally. The slides call this case isoelastisch.
  • Elastic (elastisch), \(\varepsilon < -1\): quantity changes more than proportionally.

Unlike the slope of the demand curve, the elasticity does not depend on the units of measurement (maßeinheitsunabhängig), slides 349 and 350.

Determinants (Determinanten), slides 357 to 360:

  • Substitutes (Substitutionsmöglichkeiten): without close substitutes demand is inelastic (rabies vaccine after a bite). One brand of salt is a near perfect substitute for another, so demand for a single brand is elastic.
  • Budget share (Budgetanteil): a small share (salt, dish soap) means a small income effect and less elastic demand. Rent is a large share with a large income effect.
  • Direction of the income effect: normal goods are more price elastic than inferior goods, because income and substitution effects reinforce each other.
  • Time (Zeit): demand is more elastic in the long run. After a fuel price rise, car pools, moving closer to work, or buying an efficient car take time.
Good or service (slide 351)Price elasticity
Green peas-2.8
Air travel (vacation)-1.9
Frying chickens-1.8
Beer-1.2
Marijuana-1.0
Movies-0.9
Air travel (non-vacation)-0.8
Shoes-0.7
Cigarettes-0.3
Theatre, opera-0.2
Local telephone calls-0.1

Short-run estimates; some are midpoints of a range. Note the two air travel rows: non-vacation trips are harder to replace or postpone, so demand is less elastic.

IdeaWelfare: CV and EV

Many policies act like price changes. To name winners and losers, the lecture measures the welfare effect (Wohlfahrtseffekt) of a price change in money (slide 361). Take a rise in \(p_1\) from \(p_1^a\) to \(p_1^b\), with \(p_2 = 1\) fixed and income \(m'\).

  • Compensating variation (kompensatorische Variation, CV): the money you must give the consumer after the price rise so that she is exactly as well off as before. Graph: shift the new, steeper budget line (Budgetgerade) out in parallel until it touches the old indifference curve (Indifferenzkurve) \(u_1\), slides 362 to 366.
  • Equivalent variation (äquivalente Variation, EV): the money you must take from the consumer before the price rise so that she is as well off as after it. Graph: shift the old budget line in parallel until it touches the new indifference curve \(u_2\), slides 367 to 371.

Both turn a utility change into euros. CV uses the new prices and the old utility level. EV uses the old prices and the new utility level. Because of the income effect, the two numbers generally differ.

Slide example (slides 372 to 375): \(U = x_1^{1/2}x_2^{1/2}\), \(m = 100\), \(p_2 = 1\), and \(p_1\) rises from 1 to 2. Utility falls from 50 to \(5\sqrt{50} \approx 35.36\). Result: CV = 41.42 and EV = 29.29. The algebra is on card 0.10.

Reading (slides 374 and 375): with 41.42 more income she reaches her old utility despite the higher price. Losing 29.29 of income at the old prices hurts her exactly as much as the price rise.

FormulaElasticity, revenue, CV, EV

Price elasticity of demand (slide 348)

\[ \varepsilon = \frac{\Delta Q / Q}{\Delta P / P} \] \[ \varepsilon = \frac{P}{Q}\cdot\frac{1}{\text{slope}} \]

Slope (Steigung) means \(\Delta P / \Delta Q\) of the demand curve in the price-quantity diagram. General definition and growth-rate form: see 0.6.

Elasticity and revenue (Umsatz), slide 352To raise revenue
\(|\varepsilon| > 1\), elasticCut the price
\(|\varepsilon| < 1\), inelasticRaise the price
\(|\varepsilon| = 1\)Revenue is at its maximum

Why: \(MR = P(1 - 1/|\varepsilon|)\), derived on 0.8.

Compensating variation (slide 366)

\[ CV = m'' - m' \] \[ m'' = p_1^b x_1^c + x_2^c \]

\(x^c\): optimal bundle on the old indifference curve \(u_1\) at the new prices.

Equivalent variation (slide 371)

\[ EV = m' - m'' \] \[ m'' = p_1^a x_1^c + x_2^c \]

\(x^c\): optimal bundle on the new indifference curve \(u_2\) at the old prices. \(m'\) is the original income. The slides reuse the symbol \(m''\) for both cases.

ExampleBus tickets: revenue and elasticity

Demand for bus rides in a small town (slides 353 to 356), with \(P\) in cents per ride and \(Q\) in rides per day:

Demand (Nachfrage)

\[ P = 100 - \frac{Q}{10} \] \[ Q = 1000 - 10P \]
  1. Quantity at \(P = 50\): \(Q = 1000 - 500 = 500\) rides per day.
  2. Revenue: 50 cents times 500 rides is 25,000 cents, so 250 EUR per day.
  3. Slope: \(\Delta P / \Delta Q = -1/10\), so \(1/\text{slope} = -10\).
  4. Elasticity: \[ \varepsilon = \frac{50}{500}\cdot(-10) = -1 \]
  5. Decision: \(|\varepsilon| = 1\), so revenue is at its maximum. Raising or cutting the price lowers revenue.

Check: \(R = P(1000 - 10P)\) and \(dR/dP = 1000 - 20P = 0\) at \(P = 50\). On a linear demand curve the elasticity changes along the line: at point K (\(P = 75\), \(Q = 250\)) it is \(-3\). See 0.8.

PitfallsElasticity and welfare traps
  • Slope is not elasticity: fuel demand at \(P = 3\) EUR per litre and \(Q = 50\) has slope \(-0.02\). Priced per gallon (about 4.55 litres), the price is 13.638 and the slope \(-0.0909\). The elasticity is \(-3\) in both cases (slide 350).
  • Compare absolute values: "more elastic" means a larger \(|\varepsilon|\). Green peas (\(-2.8\)) are more elastic than local calls (\(-0.1\)).
  • Isoelastisch: slide 348 uses it for \(\varepsilon = -1\). Most textbooks call that unit elastic and use isoelastic for a curve with the same elasticity at every point.
  • CV and EV differ: for a price rise of a normal good, CV is larger than EV (41.42 against 29.29). They coincide only without an income effect (quasilinear utility).
  • Typo on slide 375: it prints \(100 - 71.71\). The correct term is \(50\sqrt{2} \approx 70.71\), so EV = 29.29 is right.
Macro linkElasticities in macro
  • IS-LM slopes: the more investment reacts to the interest rate, the flatter the IS curve. In the classic LM curve (Mankiw), the more money demand reacts to the interest rate, the flatter the LM curve.
  • Marshall-Lerner condition: a real depreciation improves the trade balance only if export and import volumes react strongly enough to the real exchange rate. Quantities adjust slowly (the time determinant), so the trade balance can first worsen: the J-curve.
  • Consumer price index (Verbraucherpreisindex): a fixed-basket index ignores substitution and overstates the rise in the cost of living. The ideal measure is the CV idea: the income that keeps utility constant. In the slide example the old basket (50, 50) costs 150 at the new prices (+50%), but 141.42 (+41.42%) keeps utility at 50.
IdeaTwo periods, one budget
