Intertemporal choice (intertemporale Entscheidungen) reuses the standard consumer model with redefined goods: good 1 is consumption today \(c_1\), good 2 is consumption tomorrow \(c_2\) (slide 377). This lets us analyse saving, borrowing, and investing.

  • Endowment (Anfangsausstattung): incomes \(m_1\) and \(m_2\). Without saving or borrowing, \((c_1, c_2) = (m_1, m_2)\).
  • Interest rate (Zins) \(r\): the rate at which money moves between periods. It plays the role of the price ratio. Prices are fixed at \(p_1 = p_2 = 1\), so inflation is ignored (slide 379).
  • Future value (Zukunftswert): \(m_2 + (1+r)m_1\), the most you can consume in period 2 by saving all of \(m_1\).
  • Present value (Gegenwartswert, Barwert): \(m_1 + m_2/(1+r)\), the most you can consume today by borrowing against all of \(m_2\).
  • Saver (Sparer, Gläubiger): \(c_1 < m_1\). Lends \(m_1 - c_1\) and gets it back plus interest \(r(m_1 - c_1)\).
  • Borrower (Kreditnehmer, Schuldner): \(c_1 > m_1\). Borrows \(c_1 - m_1\) and repays it plus interest \(r(c_1 - m_1)\).

The budget line passes through the endowment with slope \(-(1+r)\): giving up one unit of \(c_1\) buys \(1 + r\) units of \(c_2\). Left of the endowment the consumer saves, right of it she borrows (slides 387 to 389).

Time preference (Zeitpräferenz): the slope of the indifference curves shows impatience. Steep curves mean an impatient (ungeduldig) consumer who needs much extra \(c_2\) to give up one unit of \(c_1\). Her tangency lies to the lower right, so she tends to borrow. Flat curves mean a patient (geduldig) consumer who tends to save (slides 390 to 392).

Slide 398: most people prefer 10 EUR today to 10 EUR tomorrow (Gegenwartspräferenz). Discount factors (Diskontfaktoren) differ across people and can be measured in experiments. Impulsivity can make choices inconsistent, like a New Year's sport resolution that ends on the couch.

FormulaIntertemporal budget line

Future values (Zukunftswerte), slide 385

\[ (1+r)c_1 + c_2 = (1+r)m_1 + m_2 \]

Present values (Gegenwartswerte), slide 385

\[ c_1 + \frac{c_2}{1+r} = m_1 + \frac{m_2}{1+r} \]

Line with slope \(-(1+r)\), slide 387

\[ c_2 = (1+r)m_1 + m_2 - (1+r)c_1 \]

Saving form (Sparen vs. Kredit), slide 389

\[ c_2 = m_2 + (1+r)(m_1 - c_1) \]

Corner points, slides 379 and 380

\[ c_1^{\max} = m_1 + \frac{m_2}{1+r} \] \[ c_2^{\max} = m_2 + (1+r)m_1 \]

Optimum: tangency (slide 392)

\[ \left|\frac{dc_2}{dc_1}\right|_{U = \text{const}} = 1 + r \]

Both budget forms describe the same line, once in period 1 euros and once in period 2 euros. Discounting and present value: see 0.6. Lagrange method for the optimum: see 0.7.

IdeaWhen the interest rate changes

A change in \(r\) rotates the budget line around the endowment \((m_1, m_2)\), because the endowment stays affordable at any rate. A fall in \(r\) makes the line flatter (slides 393 to 396).

  • Substitution effect (Substitutionseffekt): a lower \(r\) makes \(c_1\) cheaper relative to \(c_2\). It raises \(c_1\) and lowers \(c_2\) for everyone.
  • Income effect (Einkommenseffekt), saver: less interest income. The saver is poorer, so \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) both fall.
  • Income effect, borrower: cheaper debt. The borrower is richer, so \(c_1\) and \(c_2\) both rise.
Fall in \(r\)Result
Saver\(c_2\) falls. The two effects pull \(c_1\) in opposite directions; on slide 394 \(c_1\) rises. If she stays a saver, she is worse off.
BorrowerBoth effects raise \(c_1\), so she borrows more. She stays a borrower and is better off (slide 396). The effect on \(c_2\) is ambiguous.

Why the borrower stays a borrower: after the fall in \(r\), every saving point on the new line lies below the old line. She could afford those points before and chose her old bundle, which is still affordable. For a rise in \(r\) the signs flip: savers gain, borrowers lose. Summary on slide 397.

ExamplePresent value example

Slide 386: income \(m_1 = 50{,}000\) EUR today and \(m_2 = 60{,}000\) EUR in the future. Savings earn \(r = 0.2\).

  1. Save all of today's income: \(1.2 \cdot 50{,}000 = 60{,}000\) extra tomorrow. Maximum \(c_2 = 60{,}000 + 60{,}000 = 120{,}000\) EUR (future value).
  2. Borrow the present value of future income: \(60{,}000 / 1.2 = 50{,}000\) today. Maximum \(c_1 = 50{,}000 + 50{,}000 = 100{,}000\) EUR (present value).
  3. Slope: \(-120{,}000 / 100{,}000 = -1.2 = -(1+r)\).
  4. A saver's choice (added illustration): with \(c_1 = 40{,}000\) she saves 10,000 and gets back 12,000, so \(c_2 = 72{,}000\) EUR.

Check: present value of consumption

\[ 40{,}000 + \frac{72{,}000}{1.2} = 100{,}000 \]

The slide writes \(M_1, M_2, C_1, C_2\) for \(m_1, m_2, c_1, c_2\). Present value of lifetime income equals present value of consumption.

PitfallsIntertemporal traps
  • Pivot point: a change in \(r\) rotates the line around the endowment, not around an axis intercept. Both intercepts move.
  • Discount the right terms: in the present value form divide period 2 amounts by \(1+r\). In the future value form multiply period 1 amounts by \(1+r\).
  • Interest versus repayment: the saver earns interest \(r(m_1 - c_1)\) but gets back \((1+r)(m_1 - c_1)\) in total.
  • No sure sign for savers: a lower \(r\) does not always raise a saver's \(c_1\). Income and substitution effects work against each other.
  • Real rate: with \(p_1 = p_2 = 1\), \(r\) is a real interest rate. The slides contain no further inflation content.
Macro linkTwo-period model in macro
  • Consumption function: Fisher's two-period model says consumption depends on the present value of lifetime income, not only on current income. This underlies the permanent income hypothesis (Friedman) and the life-cycle hypothesis (Modigliani).
  • Euler equation: with \(U = u(c_1) + \beta u(c_2)\) the tangency becomes \(u'(c_1) = \beta(1+r)u'(c_2)\), the consumption block of dynamic macro models.
  • Ricardian equivalence: a debt-financed tax cut today means higher taxes later. The present value of disposable income is unchanged, so consumption stays the same. It fails with borrowing constraints (Kreditbeschränkungen) or myopic households.
  • Real interest rate: households react to the real rate, \(r \approx i - \pi^e\) (Fisher equation). Because income and substitution effects oppose each other for savers, the effect of \(r\) on saving is ambiguous in theory.
IdeaLotteries and risk attitudes

Decisions under uncertainty (Entscheidungen unter Unsicherheit) are modelled as lotteries (Lotterien): possible states of the world (Zustände der Welt), their payoffs, and their probabilities (slide 401).

  • Expected value (Erwartungswert): the probability-weighted average payoff. A higher expected value helps, but it cannot be the only criterion (slide 402).
  • St. Petersburg paradox: a fair coin is tossed until heads first appears. One toss pays 1 EUR, two pay 2 EUR, three pay 4 EUR, and the prize doubles with every further toss. The game ends at toss \(k\) with probability \((1/2)^k\) and pays \(2^{k-1}\) EUR, so every term of the expected value equals \(\tfrac12\) and the sum is infinite. Yet people would pay only a small fee to play (slide 403).
  • Expected utility (Erwartungsnutzen): von Neumann and Morgenstern: people choose the lottery with the highest probability-weighted sum of utilities. Utility is usually not linear in money, so the ranking by expected utility can differ from the ranking by expected value. The utility function here has cardinal meaning (slide 404). Calculations: see 0.9.
  • Risk aversion (Risikoaversion): \(U(EV) > EU\): the sure expected value beats the lottery. Marginal utility (Grenznutzen) falls with wealth: concave utility.
  • Risk loving (Risikofreude): \(U(EV) < EU\). Marginal utility rises: convex utility.
  • Risk neutrality (Risikoneutralität): \(U(EV) = EU\). Marginal utility is constant: linear utility.

A fair lottery (faire Lotterie) has an expected value of 0. A risk-averse person rejects it, a risk lover accepts it, and a risk-neutral person is indifferent (slide 411).

Slides 406 to 410: a 50:50 lottery over 90 EUR and 0 EUR with \(U(90) = 12\) and \(U(0) = 2\) has EV = 45 EUR and EU = 7. Compare \(U(45)\) with 7 to classify the person.

IdeaInsurance

A risk-averse person rejects fair lotteries, so she should be willing to sell her risk to a risk-neutral buyer at a good price. That is the principle of insurance (Versicherung), slide 412.

  • Certainty equivalent (Sicherheitsäquivalent): the sure amount with the same expected utility as the lottery (slide 415, definitions on 0.9).
  • Reservation price (Reservationspreis): the most she pays for full cover: initial wealth minus certainty equivalent.
  • Risk premium (Risikoprämie): what the insurer expects to earn above the expected payout, the reward for taking the risk.
  • Contingent consumption (zustandsabhängige Auszahlungen): treat consumption in each state as its own good, like \(c_1, c_2\) in section 8. Axes: \(C_a\) (accident) and \(C_{na}\) (no accident). Buying cover \(K\) (Versicherungssumme) at \(\gamma\) per euro moves consumption from the good state to the bad state (slides 416 to 420).
  • Full insurance (Vollversicherung): in a competitive market expected profits are zero, so \(\gamma = \pi_a\). Then \(MU(C_a) = MU(C_{na})\), so \(C_a = C_{na}\): she insures fully (slide 423).
  • Why insurers can be risk neutral: risk pooling (Risikopooling). Pooling many statistically independent risks lowers the variance of total payouts (law of large numbers, Gesetz der großen Zahlen). Fire is easier to insure than floods, which hit many people at once (slide 424).
  • What to insure: insurance usually has a negative expected value for the buyer (payouts plus administrative costs). So insure only large risks. Many people over-insure small risks (travel cancellation, bicycles) and under-insure large ones such as occupational disability (Berufsunfähigkeit), slide 425.
FormulaContingent consumption

Setting (slide 417): wealth \(m\), loss \(L\) in an accident, \(\pi_a = 0.01\), \(\pi_{na} = 0.99\), cover \(K\) at price \(\gamma\) per euro of cover.

Consumption per state (slide 419)

\[ C_{na} = m - \gamma K \] \[ C_a = m - L - \gamma K + K \] \[ C_a = m - L + (1-\gamma)K \]

Budget line, \(K\) eliminated (slides 419, 420)

\[ C_{na} = \frac{m - \gamma L}{1-\gamma} - \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\,C_a \]

Slope \(-\gamma/(1-\gamma)\). The line passes through the endowment \((C_a, C_{na}) = (m - L, m)\) and hits the \(C_a\) axis at \((m - \gamma L)/\gamma\).

Expected utility and GRS (slide 421)

\[ EU = \pi_a U(C_a) + \pi_{na} U(C_{na}) \] \[ \frac{dC_{na}}{dC_a} = -\frac{\pi_a}{\pi_{na}}\cdot\frac{MU(C_a)}{MU(C_{na})} \]

Optimum: tangency (slide 422)

\[ \frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma} = \frac{\pi_a}{\pi_{na}}\cdot\frac{MU(C_a)}{MU(C_{na})} \]

Fair premium: zero expected profit (slide 423)

\[ \gamma K - \pi_a K - \pi_{na}\cdot 0 = 0 \] \[ (\gamma - \pi_a)K = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \gamma = \pi_a \]

With \(\gamma = \pi_a\) the left side equals \(\pi_a/\pi_{na}\), so \(MU(C_a) = MU(C_{na})\). Falling marginal utility then forces \(C_a = C_{na}\), which means \(K = L\).

ExampleReservation price for insurance

Slides 412 to 415: wealth 700 EUR. With probability \(\tfrac13\) she loses 600 EUR. From the utility curve: \(U(100) = 18\), \(U(700) = 36\).

  1. Expected utility without insurance: \[ EU = \tfrac13 U(100) + \tfrac23 U(700) \] \[ EU = \tfrac13\cdot 18 + \tfrac23\cdot 36 = 30 \]
  2. Expected wealth: \[ \tfrac13\cdot 100 + \tfrac23\cdot 700 = 500 \]
  3. Certainty equivalent: a sure 370 EUR gives the same utility, \(U(370) = 30\).
  4. Reservation price: \(700 - 370 = 330\) EUR for full cover.
  5. Expected payout: \(\tfrac13\cdot 600 = 200\) EUR, the fair premium.
  6. Risk premium: \(330 - 200 = 130\) EUR, the same as \(500 - 370\).

With the fair premium of 200 EUR she holds a sure 500 EUR, and \(U(500) > 30\) because the curve is concave (slide 414). Any premium strictly between 200 and 330 EUR leaves both her and a risk-neutral insurer better off.

PitfallsUncertainty traps

Expected value ranking is not expected utility ranking (slides 402 and 405). Wealth 10,000 EUR, \(U(M) = \sqrt{M}\), fair coin:

Lottery: heads / tailsEV and EU
1: +100 / -0.50 EUREV 49.75, EU 100.248
2: +200 / -100 EUREV 50, EU 100.247
3: +20,000 / -10,000 EUREV 5,000, EU 86.603
  • Reading the table: without a lottery EU is \(\sqrt{10{,}000} = 100\). So she accepts lotteries 1 and 2 and rejects lottery 3, the one with the highest EV.
  • Typo on slide 405: \(EU_2\) shows \(\sqrt{1000 + 200}\). The correct term is \(\sqrt{10{,}000 + 200}\); the result 100.247 is right.
  • Two views of one number: slide 415 computes the risk premium from the insurer's side (\(330 - 200\)). It equals EV minus certainty equivalent (\(500 - 370\)), the definition on 0.9.
  • Full cover needs a fair premium: the result \(K = L\) rests on \(\gamma = \pi_a\). With a markup for costs, full insurance is generally no longer optimal.
Macro linkRisk in macro
  • Risk premia: risk-averse lenders demand compensation, so firms borrow at the policy rate plus a risk premium (Blanchard and Illing). When risk premia jump, as in the 2008 crisis, investment falls even if the central bank cuts its rate.
  • Precautionary saving (Vorsichtssparen): when future income is uncertain, households save more than under certainty. Strictly, this needs convex marginal utility (prudence), which standard functions such as log utility have.
  • Social insurance: unemployment insurance moves income into the bad state, as in the contingent consumption model. It smooths consumption and acts as an automatic stabilizer.
  • Deposit insurance (Einlagensicherung): it removes the reason for bank runs. Bank failures in a crisis are correlated, like floods on slide 424, so they are hard to insure by private pooling alone.
QuestionMicro 7.1

Bus demand is \(Q = 1000 - 10P\), with \(P\) in cents per ride (slides 353 to 356). Compute the price elasticity and daily revenue at \(P = 75\) and at \(P = 25\). In which direction should the company move the price in each case to raise revenue?

Show answer

At \(P = 75\): \(Q = 250\) and \(\varepsilon = \frac{75}{250}\cdot(-10) = -3\). Demand is elastic. Revenue is 18,750 cents, so 187.50 EUR. Cut the price.

At \(P = 25\): \(Q = 750\) and \(\varepsilon = \frac{25}{750}\cdot(-10) = -\tfrac13\). Demand is inelastic. Revenue is again 187.50 EUR. Raise the price.

Both moves lead toward \(P = 50\), where \(\varepsilon = -1\) and revenue peaks at 250 EUR per day.

QuestionMicro 7.2

In the slide example (slides 372 to 375), \(p_1\) rises from 1 to 2 and you get CV = 41.42 and EV = 29.29. What does each number mean? At which prices and on which indifference curve is each one computed, and why is CV the larger one?

Show answer

CV: the extra income she needs after the price rise to reach her old utility of 50. It is computed at the new prices (\(p_1 = 2\)) on the old indifference curve.

EV: the income cut at the old prices that leaves her as badly off as the price rise does, at utility \(5\sqrt{50} \approx 35.36\). It is computed at the old prices (\(p_1 = 1\)) on the new indifference curve.

Both measure the same utility drop, from 50 to about 35.36. CV values it at the new prices, where reaching any utility level costs more money, so CV is larger. Algebra: card 0.10.

QuestionMicro 8.1

Use the setting of slide 386: \(m_1 = 50{,}000\) EUR, \(m_2 = 60{,}000\) EUR, \(r = 0.2\). A consumer chooses \(c_1 = 60{,}000\) EUR. Is she a saver or a borrower? How much does she repay, and what is \(c_2\)?

Show answer

\(c_1 > m_1\), so she is a borrower. She borrows 10,000 EUR and repays \(1.2 \cdot 10{,}000 = 12{,}000\) EUR, of which 2,000 EUR is interest.

\(c_2 = 60{,}000 - 12{,}000 = 48{,}000\) EUR.

Check: \(60{,}000 + 48{,}000/1.2 = 100{,}000\), the present value of her income.

QuestionMicro 8.2

The interest rate falls. Use income and substitution effects to explain what happens to \(c_1\), \(c_2\), and welfare for (a) a saver and (b) a borrower (slides 393 to 397).

Show answer

The substitution effect raises \(c_1\) and lowers \(c_2\) for both, because \(c_1\) becomes cheaper relative to \(c_2\).

(a) Saver: she earns less interest and is poorer, so the income effect lowers both \(c_1\) and \(c_2\). \(c_2\) falls for sure; \(c_1\) can go either way. If she stays a saver, she is worse off.

(b) Borrower: debt is cheaper and she is richer, so the income effect raises both. \(c_1\) rises for sure and she borrows more; \(c_2\) is ambiguous. She stays a borrower and is better off, because her old bundle is still affordable.

QuestionMicro 9.1

A 50:50 lottery pays 90 EUR or 0 EUR, with \(U(90) = 12\) and \(U(0) = 2\) (slide 406). A person is indifferent between this lottery and a sure 30 EUR. Is she risk averse, risk neutral, or risk loving? What is her risk premium?

Show answer

\(EU = 0.5\cdot 12 + 0.5\cdot 2 = 7\), so \(U(30) = 7\). The expected value is 45 EUR.

Utility rises with money, so \(U(45) > U(30) = 7\). She prefers the sure expected value to the lottery: she is risk averse.

Her certainty equivalent is 30 EUR, so the risk premium is \(45 - 30 = 15\) EUR (definitions on 0.9).

QuestionMicro 9.2

Slide 417: accident probability \(\pi_a = 0.01\), loss \(L\), wealth \(m\). Cover costs \(\gamma\) per euro. In a competitive insurance market, what is \(\gamma\)? How much cover \(K\) does a risk-averse person buy, and what does she consume in each state?

Show answer

Zero expected profit: \((\gamma - \pi_a)K = 0\), so \(\gamma = 0.01\).

Then \(\gamma/(1-\gamma) = \pi_a/\pi_{na}\), and the tangency condition requires \(MU(C_a) = MU(C_{na})\). With falling marginal utility this means \(C_a = C_{na}\), so \(K = L\): full insurance.

\(C_{na} = m - 0.01L\) and \(C_a = m - L + 0.99L = m - 0.01L\). The premium \(0.01L\) equals the expected loss.

IdeaProduction function and isoquants

A technology (Technologie) turns inputs (Produktionsfaktoren) such as labor, capital, land, and raw materials into output. The production function (Produktionsfunktion) gives the maximum output an input bundle can produce with the best available technology: \(y = f(x_1, x_2)\) on slides 429 to 458, \(Q = F(K, L)\) from slide 462 on.

  • Production possibility set (Produktionsmöglichkeitenmenge): all feasible input and output plans. Plans on the production function are technically efficient (technisch effizient). Plans below it waste inputs (slide 432).
  • Isoquant (Output-Isoquante): all input bundles that just produce a given output. Several isoquants form a map (Isoquantenschar). The full map carries the same information as the production function, like indifference curves and utility (slide 435).
  • Cobb-Douglas: smooth isoquants that bend toward the origin. Slide 433 uses \(y = 2x_1^{1/3}x_2^{1/3}\).
  • Leontief (limitationale Technologie): \(y = \min\{ax_1, bx_2\}\). Inputs work only in fixed proportions. Isoquants are L-shaped with corners on the ray \(ax_1 = bx_2\). More of one input alone adds nothing.
  • Perfect substitutes (perfekte Substitute): \(y = ax_1 + bx_2\). Isoquants are straight lines. In slide 441, \(y = x_1 + 3x_2\), one unit of \(x_2\) replaces three units of \(x_1\).
  • Monotonicity (Monotonie): more of an input never lowers output (slides 456 and 457).
  • Convexity (Konvexität): if two bundles each produce \(y\), any weighted average of them produces at least \(y\). Then the TRS falls in absolute value as you move along an isoquant toward more \(x_1\) (slide 458).
  • Short run and long run (kurze und lange Frist): in the short run at least one input, such as machines or land, cannot be adjusted. In the long run all inputs are variable (slide 459).

Slide 440 titles its Leontief example \(\min\{x_1, x_2\}\), but the corners it draws, (2, 1), (4, 2), and (6, 3), lie on \(x_1 = 2x_2\). That fits \(\min\{x_1, 2x_2\}\). (slides 428 to 441, 456 to 459)

IdeaMarginal product, returns to scale, TRS

Three questions about any technology: what one more unit of one input adds, what happens when all inputs grow together, and how inputs trade off at constant output.

  • Marginal product (Grenzprodukt), \(MP_i\): the extra output from a small increase in input \(i\), all other inputs fixed (slide 442). It plays the role of marginal utility in consumer theory. The marginal product of one input usually depends on how much of the other inputs is used (slide 443).
  • Law of diminishing returns (Gesetz des abnehmenden Grenzertrags): with the other inputs fixed, the output gain from more of one input shrinks, at least beyond some point (slide 444). Kitchen example (slide 445): a second cook allows specialization, so output first rises at an increasing rate. With 25 cooks they get in each other's way at the given stoves and pans.
  • Returns to scale (Skalenerträge): scale all inputs by \(k > 1\). If output grows by exactly, more than, or less than the factor \(k\), returns to scale are constant (konstant), increasing (steigend), or decreasing (abnehmend), slides 446 to 448. They can change along the output range (slide 450).
  • Two different ideas: diminishing marginal product varies one input. Returns to scale vary all inputs in proportion. An airline that doubles only its pilots hits diminishing returns to pilots. Doubling pilots, planes, and ticket staff together can still give constant or increasing returns to scale (slides 452 and 453). The Cobb-Douglas check is on 0.7.
  • Technical rate of substitution (technische Rate der Substitution, TRS): the rate at which you can swap one input for another without changing output. It is the slope of the isoquant and equals \(-MP_1/MP_2\) (slides 454 and 455). Derivation from \(dy = 0\): see 0.7.
FormulaTechnology in formulas

Production function (Produktionsfunktion), slides 429 and 462

\[ y = f(x_1, x_2) \qquad Q = F(K, L) \]

Marginal product (Grenzprodukt), slides 442 and 443

\[ MP_i = \frac{\partial y}{\partial x_i} \] \[ MP_L = \frac{\partial F}{\partial L} \qquad MP_K = \frac{\partial F}{\partial K} \] \[ \text{diminishing: } \frac{\partial MP_i}{\partial x_i} = \frac{\partial^2 y}{\partial x_i^2} < 0 \]

Returns to scale (Skalenerträge), \(k > 1\), slides 446 and 447

\[ f(kx_1, kx_2) = k\,f(x_1, x_2) \;\text{: constant} \] \[ f(kx_1, kx_2) > k\,f(x_1, x_2) \;\text{: increasing} \] \[ f(kx_1, kx_2) < k\,f(x_1, x_2) \;\text{: decreasing} \]

TRS: slope of the isoquant, slides 454 and 455

\[ dy = MP_1\,dx_1 + MP_2\,dx_2 = 0 \] \[ TRS = \frac{dx_2}{dx_1} = -\frac{MP_1}{MP_2} \]

Three standard technologies

\[ \text{Cobb-Douglas: } y = A\,x_1^{a}x_2^{b} \] \[ \text{Leontief: } y = \min\{a x_1,\, b x_2\} \] \[ \text{Substitutes: } y = a x_1 + b x_2,\quad TRS = -\tfrac{a}{b} \]

Partial derivatives of Cobb-Douglas: see 0.5. Returns to scale from the sum of exponents \(a + b\), with the slide 451 example: see 0.7.

ExampleCobb-Douglas at two bundles

Slide 433: \(y = 2x_1^{1/3}x_2^{1/3}\), evaluated at the bundles (8, 1) and (8, 8).

Output (slide 433)

\[ f(8, 1) = 2\cdot 2\cdot 1 = 4 \qquad f(8, 8) = 2\cdot 2\cdot 2 = 8 \]

Marginal products at (8, 1)

\[ MP_1 = \tfrac{2}{3}\,x_1^{-2/3}x_2^{1/3} = \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot\tfrac{1}{4}\cdot 1 = \tfrac{1}{6} \] \[ MP_2 = \tfrac{2}{3}\,x_1^{1/3}x_2^{-2/3} = \tfrac{2}{3}\cdot 2\cdot 1 = \tfrac{4}{3} \]

TRS at (8, 1) and at (8, 8)

\[ TRS_{(8,1)} = -\frac{1/6}{4/3} = -\frac{1}{8} \qquad TRS_{(8,8)} = -1 \]
  • At (8, 1), \(x_2\) is scarce and its marginal product is high: one unit of \(x_2\) is worth 8 units of \(x_1\). At (8, 8) the inputs trade one for one.
  • Raising \(x_2\) eightfold, from 1 to 8, only doubles output from 4 to 8: diminishing marginal product of \(x_2\).
  • Doubling both inputs, from (8, 1) to (16, 2), gives \(4\cdot 2^{2/3} \approx 6.35 < 8\). Returns to scale are decreasing, because \(\tfrac13 + \tfrac13 < 1\) (see 0.7).
Macro linkProduction functions in macro
  • Aggregate production function (gesamtwirtschaftliche Produktionsfunktion): macro writes \(Y = F(K, N)\) (Blanchard and Illing, labor is \(N\)) or \(Y = F(K, L)\) (Mankiw). It is the same object as here, applied to a whole economy.
  • Solow model: constant returns to scale let you write output per worker as a function of capital per worker, \(Y/N = F(K/N, 1)\). Diminishing marginal product of capital is why capital accumulation alone ends in a steady state.
  • Cobb-Douglas workhorse: \(Y = K^{\alpha}N^{1-\alpha}\), exponents summing to 1. Its marginal products and growth accounting are on 0.5.
  • Technology as a shift: better technology (total factor productivity, \(A\)) gives more output from the same inputs, like cars made with today's technology versus that of 1970 (slide 428). In the Solow model, lasting growth in output per worker comes only from technological progress.
  • Fixed capital: short-run and medium-run macro models treat the capital stock as given and labor as the variable input, much like the micro short run (slide 459).
QuestionMicro 10.1

Slide 441 uses the perfect-substitutes technology \(y = x_1 + 3x_2\). What is the TRS? How many units of \(x_1\) replace one unit of \(x_2\), and where does the isoquant \(y = 18\) cross the axes?

Show answer

\(MP_1 = 1\) and \(MP_2 = 3\), so \(TRS = -MP_1/MP_2 = -\tfrac13\) at every bundle. The isoquants are straight lines.

Giving up one unit of \(x_2\) costs 3 units of output, so 3 units of \(x_1\) replace it.

The isoquant \(x_1 + 3x_2 = 18\) crosses the axes at \(x_1 = 18\) and \(x_2 = 6\), as drawn on slide 441.

QuestionMicro 10.2

An airline doubles its number of pilots and keeps planes and ticket staff unchanged. Output rises by much less than double. Does this show decreasing returns to scale (slides 452 and 453)?

Show answer

No. Changing one input with the others fixed tests the marginal product. The result shows diminishing marginal product of pilots.

Returns to scale ask what happens when all inputs grow in the same proportion: pilots, planes, and ticket staff together. The airline can still have constant or increasing returns to scale.

A Cobb-Douglas function with exponents 0.6 and 0.6 shows both at once: each marginal product falls, yet returns to scale increase (see 0.7).

IdeaCosts in the short run

In the short run some inputs are fixed, so costs split into a fixed and a variable part (slide 461). The slides use a laundry, Rainer's cleaning business (Rainers Reinigung), as the running example.

  • Fixed costs (Fixkosten), \(FC\): costs of the fixed inputs. They do not change with output in the short run. Rainer owns his washing machines. Their rental value is an opportunity cost (Opportunitätskosten): 120 machine hours at 0.25 EUR gives \(FC = rK_0 = 30\) EUR (slide 463).
  • Variable costs (variable Kosten), \(VC\): costs of the variable inputs, here labor at 10 EUR per hour, so \(VC = wL\). At zero output they are zero (slides 464 and 465).
  • Total costs (Gesamtkosten), \(TC = FC + VC\): the \(TC\) curve is the \(VC\) curve shifted up by \(FC\). Both have the same slope (slide 465).
  • Shape of \(VC\): while the marginal product of labor rises (up to 4 workers), each extra load needs less extra labor, so \(VC\) rises at a falling rate. After that, diminishing marginal product makes \(VC\) rise at a growing rate (slide 466).
  • Average costs (Durchschnittskosten): \(AFC\), \(AVC\), and \(ATC\) are fixed, variable, and total costs per unit (slide 467). \(AFC\) keeps falling as fixed costs spread over more units.
  • Marginal cost (Grenzkosten), \(MC\): the extra cost of one more unit, the slope of \(TC\) and of \(VC\) (slide 468). \(MC\) falls until diminishing marginal product sets in, then rises (slide 469).
  • \(MC\) cuts the averages at their minimum: while \(MC < ATC\) the average falls, while \(MC > ATC\) it rises (slide 470). The same holds for \(AVC\). Why: see 0.8.
IdeaLong run: the cheapest input mix

In the long run all inputs are variable, so the firm also chooses its mix of \(K\) and \(L\) (slide 471).

  • Isocost line (Isokostengerade): all bundles that cost the same amount \(C\) at input prices \(r\) and \(w\). Its slope is \(-w/r\) (slides 471 and 472).
  • Two views, one answer: maximum output for given spending (slides 473 to 477) and minimum cost for a given output (slides 478 to 482) both end at the tangency of isoquant and isocost line.
  • Long-run optimum (slides 483 to 485): the isoquant is as steep as the isocost line. Equivalently, the last euro spent on each input buys the same extra output. If one input gives more output per euro, shift spending toward it.
  • Gravel example (Schotterproduktion, slides 488 to 490): the same technology meets different input prices. Low wages in Nepal make the isocost line flat, so the cheapest way to make a tonne of gravel uses a lot of labor: hand and hammer. High German wages make it steep, and the tangency moves to a capital-intensive bundle: machines.
  • Expansion path (Expansionspfad): the tangency points as spending grows (slides 491 and 492). It turns each output level into long-run total cost \(LTC(Q)\), which starts at the origin because no input is fixed (slide 493). From \(LTC\) come \(LAC\) and \(LMC\) (slide 494).
  • Returns to scale shape \(LAC\) (slide 495): constant returns mean costs proportional to output, so \(LAC\) is flat. Increasing returns make \(LAC\) fall, decreasing returns make it rise.
  • Industry structure (slides 497 to 500): minimum efficient scale (mindesteffiziente Betriebsgröße) is the output where \(LAC\) reaches its minimum. If it is a large share of the market (the slides give more than 20 percent as an example), a few firms tend to dominate. If one firm serves the market most cheaply, it is a natural monopoly (natürliches Monopol).
FormulaShort-run costs

Cost split, slides 461 to 464 (\(K_0\): fixed capital)

\[ FC = rK_0 \qquad VC = wL \] \[ TC = FC + VC = rK_0 + wL \]

Marginal cost and the marginal product of labor

\[ MC = \frac{\Delta VC}{\Delta Q} = \frac{w\,\Delta L}{\Delta Q} = \frac{w}{MP_L} \]
  • This identity explains slide 469: \(MC\) falls while \(MP_L\) rises and rises once \(MP_L\) falls.
  • Fixed costs drop out of \(MC\), because \(\Delta TC = \Delta VC\).

Definitions of \(AFC\), \(AVC\), \(ATC\), \(MC = dTC/dQ\), the proof that \(MC\) cuts \(ATC\) at its minimum, and a cost-curve graph: see 0.8.

FormulaLong-run cost minimization

Isocost line (Isokostengerade), slide 472

\[ C = rK + wL \;\Rightarrow\; K = \frac{C}{r} - \frac{w}{r}\,L \]

Cost minimum, slides 483 to 485

\[ \frac{MP_L}{MP_K} = \frac{w}{r} \iff \frac{MP_L}{w} = \frac{MP_K}{r} \] \[ \frac{MP_{X_1}}{P_{X_1}} = \frac{MP_{X_2}}{P_{X_2}} = \dots = \frac{MP_{X_N}}{P_{X_N}} \]

Lagrange problem (Lagrange-Problem), slide 487

\[ \min_{K,L,\lambda}\; rK + wL + \lambda\big(F(K, L) - Q_0\big) \] \[ r + \lambda\,MP_K = 0 \qquad w + \lambda\,MP_L = 0 \] \[ \Rightarrow\; \frac{MP_L}{MP_K} = \frac{w}{r}, \qquad F(K, L) = Q_0 \]

Long-run cost curves, slide 494

\[ LAC = \frac{LTC(Q)}{Q} \qquad LMC = \frac{dLTC}{dQ} \]

With the plus sign used on slide 487, \(\lambda\) comes out negative. Written with a minus sign, \(\lambda = w/MP_L = r/MP_K\), which is the marginal cost of output. The mirror problem, maximum output for a given budget, is on 0.5.

ExampleRainer's cleaning: cost per load

Slide 462: with fixed capital, \(L = 1, 2, \dots, 8\) workers wash \(Q = 4, 14, 27, 43, 58, 72, 81, 86\) loads per hour. \(w = 10\) EUR and \(FC = 30\) EUR, so \(VC = 10L\) and \(TC = 30 + 10L\) (slides 463 to 465).

At \(Q = 27\), \(L = 3\) (slide 464)

\[ VC = 10\cdot 3 = 30 \qquad TC = 30 + 30 = 60 \] \[ AVC = \tfrac{30}{27} \approx 1.11 \qquad ATC = \tfrac{60}{27} \approx 2.22 \]
Extra worker: \(Q\) step\(MP_L\), then \(MC = 10/MP_L\)
1st: 0 to 44, so 2.50
2nd: 4 to 1410, so 1.00
3rd: 14 to 2713, so 0.77
4th: 27 to 4316, so 0.63
5th: 43 to 5815, so 0.67
6th: 58 to 7214, so 0.71
7th: 72 to 819, so 1.11
8th: 81 to 865, so 2.00
  • \(MC\) is lowest where \(MP_L\) is highest, at the 4th worker, on the step from 27 to 43 loads. After that, diminishing marginal product drives \(MC\) up (slides 466 and 469).
  • \(AVC\) is lowest at \(Q = 72\): \(60/72 \approx 0.83\). \(ATC\) is lowest at \(Q = 81\): \(100/81 \approx 1.23\).
  • Check of slide 470: the step to 86 costs 2.00 per load, more than \(ATC\), so \(ATC\) rises to \(110/86 \approx 1.28\).

All values computed from the points on the slide 462 graph. Marginal cost here is per step, \(\Delta TC/\Delta Q\), in EUR per load.

Macro linkCosts in macro
  • Marginal cost of labor: with the simple production function \(Y = AN\) (Blanchard and Illing), one more unit of output needs \(1/A\) workers, so \(MC = W/A\). With \(A = 1\), \(MC = W\). In general \(MC = W/MP_N\), the same identity as \(w/MP_L\) here.
  • Price setting: firms set their price as a markup over this marginal cost, which gives the price-setting relation \(P = (1 + m)W\). The markup is the topic of section 13.
  • Factor substitution: with \(Q = K^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}\), cost minimization gives \(\frac{wL}{rK} = \frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\), a fixed ratio of labor cost to capital cost. When labor gets dearer relative to capital, firms use more capital per worker, as in the gravel example.
  • Menu costs (Menükosten): a small fixed cost of changing prices can make it rational to leave prices unchanged when demand shifts (Mankiw). This is one reason for sticky prices in the short run.
  • Same words, other meaning: in Blanchard and Illing, short, medium, and long run (kurze, mittlere, lange Frist) refer to which forces drive output: demand in the short run, supply and the labor market in the medium run, and growth in the long run. In micro they refer to which inputs are fixed.
QuestionMicro 11.1

Slide 486: \(MP_L = MP_K = 80\), \(r = 160\) EUR per day, \(w = 80\) EUR per day. Is the firm minimizing its costs? If not, which way should it change its input mix, and what does it save?

Show answer

Output per last euro: labor \(MP_L/w = 80/80 = 1\) unit, capital \(MP_K/r = 80/160 = 0.5\) units. They differ, so costs are not minimal.

Spend 1 EUR less on capital: output falls by 0.5 units. Spend 0.50 EUR more on labor: output rises by 0.5 units. Output is unchanged and 0.50 EUR is saved.

So use more labor and less capital. As \(L\) rises, \(MP_L\) falls; as \(K\) falls, \(MP_K\) rises, until \(MP_L/w = MP_K/r\).

QuestionMicro 11.2

Slide 472: \(r = 2\) EUR, \(w = 4\) EUR, budget \(C = 200\) EUR per day. Write the isocost line as \(K\) in terms of \(L\) and give both intercepts and the slope. What changes if the wage rises to \(w = 8\), and how does the cheapest bundle for a given output react?

Show answer

\(200 = 2K + 4L\), so \(K = 100 - 2L\). Intercepts: \(K = C/r = 100\) and \(L = C/w = 50\). Slope: \(-w/r = -2\).

With \(w = 8\): \(K = 100 - 4L\). The \(K\) intercept stays at 100, the \(L\) intercept falls to 25, and the line gets steeper (slope \(-4\)).

For a given isoquant, the steeper isocost line touches it at a point with more \(K\) and less \(L\). That is the gravel example: high-wage Germany uses machines, low-wage Nepal uses labor (slides 489 and 490).

IdeaProfit and the competitive firm
  • Why assume profit maximization (Gewinnmaximierung): you need a goal to derive testable predictions; it is not a normative claim (slides 503 and 504). Even firms that decided at random would end up looking like profit maximizers, because the market weeds out the unlucky ones. Creditors and profit-linked manager pay push the same way.
  • Economic versus accounting profit (ökonomischer und buchhalterischer Gewinn): accounting profit subtracts only explicit costs. Economic profit also subtracts implicit costs, the opportunity costs of inputs the firm owns (slide 505).
  • Slide 507: revenue 250 EUR, labor 100 EUR, and the firm's own capital could be rented out for 100 EUR. Accounting profit is 150 EUR, economic profit 50 EUR.
  • Zero economic profit is not zero income: the owners earn exactly what their resources would earn in the best alternative, a normal profit.
  • Perfect competition (vollkommener Wettbewerb), slides 510 to 513: homogeneous products (homogene Produkte), firms are price takers (Preisnehmer), free entry and exit (freier Marktein- und -austritt), and complete information (vollständige Informationen). The model also assumes no externalities and private goods (slide 515).
  • Realism: the assumptions fit some markets well, such as farm products, and others poorly. Read with care, the model still gives useful predictions (slide 514).
  • Demand facing one firm: a horizontal line at the market price. The firm can sell any amount at \(P^*\), sells nothing above it, and has no reason to go below it (slide 528). So its marginal revenue (Grenzerlös) equals the price (slide 518).
IdeaShort run, long run, invisible hand
  • Output rule: produce where \(P = MC\) on the rising part of \(MC\) (slides 518 and 519). Before that point an extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost; beyond it, less.
  • Shutdown rule (Produktionseinstellung): if the price is below the minimum of \(AVC\), produce nothing in the short run (slide 521). Above it, revenue covers all variable costs and part of the fixed costs. Producing then loses less than shutting down, which loses all of \(FC\) (slides 524 and 531).
  • Short-run supply curve (kurzfristige Angebotskurve): the rising part of \(MC\) above \(\min AVC\) (slides 522 and 523). Market supply adds the firms' quantities at each price (slides 525 to 527).
  • Break-even point (Gewinnschwelle): the lowest price without a loss, \(P = \min ATC\) (slide 530). Between \(\min AVC\) and \(\min ATC\) the firm produces at a loss.
  • Short-run equilibrium: market supply and demand set \(P^*\). Each firm earns \((P^* - ATC)\cdot Q\), which can be positive (slide 529) or negative (slide 531).
  • Long-run adjustment (Anpassung in der langen Frist), slides 532 and 533: positive economic profit attracts entry. Market supply shifts right and the price falls until economic profit is zero and \(P = \min LAC\). Losses work the other way, through exit.
  • Invisible hand (unsichtbare Hand), slides 534 and 535: in the long-run equilibrium \(P = MC\), so the last unit is worth to buyers exactly what its resources cost and no Pareto improvement is left. \(P = \min LAC\), so nothing is produced more cheaply elsewhere. Owners earn a normal profit. The market coordinates all this without a central planner, but only when the competitive assumptions hold.
FormulaProfit maximization in formulas

Economic profit (ökonomischer Gewinn), slide 505

\[ \Pi = TR - TC = P\cdot Q - TC(Q) \]

Price taker: output rule, slide 518

\[ MR = P \qquad P = MC \text{ (rising part of } MC) \]

Shutdown and break-even, slides 521 and 530

\[ P < \min AVC \;\Rightarrow\; Q = 0 \] \[ P = \min ATC \;\Rightarrow\; \Pi = 0 \]

Profit as a rectangle, slide 529

\[ \Pi = (P - ATC)\cdot Q \]

Input side, short run with fixed \(K\), slide 516

\[ \Pi = pQ - wL - rK \] \[ \frac{\partial \Pi}{\partial L} = p\,\frac{\partial Q}{\partial L} - w = 0 \] \[ \Rightarrow\; p\cdot MP_L = w \] \[ p\uparrow\; \Rightarrow\; L\uparrow \qquad w\uparrow\; \Rightarrow\; L\downarrow \]

Long-run equilibrium, slide 533

\[ P = \min LAC \qquad \Pi = 0 \]

\(p\cdot MP_L\) is the value of the marginal product (Wertgrenzprodukt). The input rule and the output rule say the same thing: \(p = w/MP_L = MC\). Shutdown and break-even on a cost-curve graph: see 0.8. Adding supply curves: see 0.10.

ExampleProfit and loss in the short run

Three price-taking firms from the slides, each at its profit-maximizing output, where \(P = MC\).

Slide 517: \(P = 18\), \(Q^* = 7.4\)

\[ TR = 18\cdot 7.4 = 133.2 \qquad TC = 120.6 \] \[ \Pi = 133.2 - 120.6 = 12.6 \]

Profit is zero at \(Q = 4.7\) and \(Q = 8.7\) and equals \(-FC = -30\) at \(Q = 0\). The maximum lies where \(TR\) and \(TC\) are equally steep.

Slide 529: \(P = 20\), \(Q_i = 80\), \(ATC = 12\)

\[ \Pi = (20 - 12)\cdot 80 = 1{,}600 - 960 = 640 \]

Slide 531: \(P = 10\), \(Q_i = 60\), \(ATC = 12\)

\[ \Pi = (10 - 12)\cdot 60 = -120 \]
  • At \(P = 10\) the firm still produces, because \(P > AVC\). Shutting down would lose all fixed costs, which are larger than 120 (slide 531).
  • Long run: the 640 profit attracts entry, the 120 loss drives exit, until \(P = \min LAC\) (slides 532 and 533).

Amounts in EUR per week. Slides 522 to 524 add the supply curve: \(\min AVC = 12\) at \(Q = 5.6\); \(P = 14\) gives \(Q = 6.4\) and \(P = 20\) gives \(Q = 7.8\).

PitfallsProfit and supply traps
  • Shutdown uses \(AVC\), break-even uses \(ATC\). Fixed costs are paid in the short run either way, so they do not affect whether to produce.
  • \(P = MC\) on the falling part of \(MC\) is a profit minimum, not a maximum (slide 519 shows the two crossings).
  • Long-run zero profit means zero economic profit. Accounting profit is still positive.
  • Supply is added horizontally: add quantities at the same price, not prices at the same quantity (see 0.10).
  • Slide 509 arithmetic: \(12{,}000 - 800 - 1{,}000{,}000 = -988{,}800\), not \(-988{,}900\) as printed. The land's opportunity cost is 1,000,000 EUR per month (printed as "1.0000.000").
Macro linkCompetitive firms in macro
  • Labor demand: a competitive firm hires until \(MP_L = w/p\), the real wage. This is the labor demand curve of the classical model in Mankiw. Capital is rented until \(MP_K\) equals the real rental rate \(R/P\).
  • Income shares: with \(Y = AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}\) and factors paid their marginal products, labor receives \((1-\alpha)Y\) and capital \(\alpha Y\). Mankiw uses this to explain why the capital share stays near 0.3 over time.
  • No profit left over: with constant returns to scale, paying every factor its marginal product uses up exactly all output (Euler's theorem in Mankiw). This is the macro version of zero economic profit in the long run.
  • Not a sum of supply curves: the aggregate supply curve in AS-AD is not the horizontal sum of firms' \(MC\) curves. Blanchard and Illing derive it from wage setting and price setting.
QuestionMicro 12.1

Slides 522 to 524: the minimum of \(AVC\) is 12 (at \(Q = 5.6\)). At \(P = 14\) the firm produces 6.4 units although the price does not cover \(ATC\). Why does it not shut down? What should it do at \(P = 11\)?

Show answer

At \(P = 14 > \min AVC = 12\), revenue covers all variable costs and part of the fixed costs. The firm makes a loss, but a smaller one than if it shut down, which would lose all fixed costs. So it produces where \(P = MC\), at 6.4 units.

At \(P = 11 < 12\), revenue does not even cover variable costs. Every unit adds to the loss, so it shuts down: \(Q = 0\), loss \(= FC\).

The short-run supply curve is the \(MC\) curve above 12.

QuestionMicro 12.2

Slides 508 and 509: Bernd nets 800 EUR a month from his rented mini-golf course in Dalmatia and could earn 800 EUR in a supermarket. On land he inherited in London he would net 12,000 EUR a month. The land would sell for 100,000,000 EUR at 1 percent interest per month. Compare accounting and economic profit. Should he move?

Show answer

Accounting profit: 800 EUR in Dalmatia, 12,000 EUR in London.

Economic profit in Dalmatia: \(800 - 800 = 0\), after the opportunity cost of his labor.

Economic profit in London also subtracts the land's opportunity cost, \(0.01\cdot 100{,}000{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000\) EUR a month: \(12{,}000 - 800 - 1{,}000{,}000 = -988{,}800\) EUR. The slide prints \(-988{,}900\), an arithmetic slip.

So no: a profit maximizer would not run a mini-golf course on that land. He does better selling or renting it out.

IdeaHow a monopolist sets its price
  • Monopoly (Monopol): a single seller of a product without close substitutes serves the whole market and has price-setting power (Preissetzungsmacht), slide 538. Whether substitutes are close is often hard to judge; the cross-price elasticity helps (slide 539).
  • The real difference to competition is not the elasticity of market demand but the demand curve the firm faces. A competitive firm faces a horizontal line. The monopolist faces the falling market demand curve (slide 540).
  • Sources of monopoly (slide 541): exclusive control of key inputs, economies of scale (falling average costs, as in power grids), patents, network economies (a good is worth more the more people use it), and government licenses.
  • Marginal revenue below price: to sell one more unit, the monopolist must cut the price on all units, not only the last one. So \(MR\) is the price of the extra unit minus the revenue lost on the earlier units, and \(MR < P\) (slides 550 to 553).
  • Slide 551: cutting the price from 60 to 50 raises sales from 100 to 150. The firm gains 2,500 EUR per week on the new units and loses 1,000 EUR on the old ones, so \(MR = 1{,}500/50 = 30 < 50\).
  • Profit rule: choose \(Q\) where \(MR = MC\), where the \(TR\) and \(TC\) curves are equally steep (slides 547 and 548). Then read the price off the demand curve. The profit maximum lies left of the revenue maximum: on slide 546, \(Q^* = 175\) against 200.
  • Only the elastic part: a monopolist never produces where demand is inelastic, because there \(MR < 0\) (slide 561).
  • Markup (Aufschlag): the gap between price and marginal cost, as a share of the price, is \(1/|\varepsilon|\). The more elastic demand, the smaller the markup. With infinite elasticity \(P = MC\), the competitive case (slides 556 and 562).
IdeaWelfare loss and monopoly policy
  • Deadweight loss (Wohlfahrtsverlust), slides 595 and 596: with constant \(LAC = LMC\), competition produces \(Q_C\) at \(P_C = MC\). A single-price monopolist (Einheitspreismonopol) sells less, \(Q^* < Q_C\), at a higher price \(P^*\). Part of the consumer surplus becomes profit \(\Pi\). The triangle \(S_1\) between demand and \(MC\), from \(Q^*\) to \(Q_C\), is lost to everyone.
  • Perfect price discrimination would produce \(Q_C\) and remove the deadweight loss, but the monopolist would capture the entire consumer surplus (slides 595 and 597).
  • Compared with what? (slide 598): if a patent creates the monopoly, the product might not exist without it. The relevant comparison is then with no product at all, and the monopoly adds \(S_2 + \Pi > 0\).
  • Natural monopoly (natürliches Monopol), slide 599: \(TC = F + MQ\), with a high fixed cost \(F\) and constant marginal cost \(M\). One firm produces any output most cheaply. But \(ATC\) always exceeds \(M\), so pricing at marginal cost, at the efficient quantity \(Q^{**}\), means a loss. Left alone, the firm sells \(Q^*\) at \(P^*\).
  • Nationalization (Verstaatlichung), slide 601: the state sets \(P = MC\) and covers the loss. Risk: weak incentives for cost-conscious management.
  • Regulation (Regulierung), slide 602: rate-of-return regulation (Renditeregulierung) or price caps aim for a price near \(ATC\). A return set too low erodes quality, one set too high keeps prices high, and rate-of-return rules invite too much capital.
  • Auctioning the monopoly right (Auktion der Monopolposition), slide 603: firms bid for a time-limited monopoly, such as waste collection. Complete contracts are hard to write and to check, and price trades off against quality.
  • Also on the list (slide 600): strict antitrust enforcement (Kartellgesetze) and laissez-faire for natural monopolies. Every option has problems; the best one depends on the case (slide 604).
FormulaMonopoly in formulas

Revenue and marginal revenue, slides 552 to 554

\[ TR = P(Q)\cdot Q \qquad MR = P + \frac{dP}{dQ}\,Q < P \]

Profit maximum (Gewinnmaximum), slide 548

\[ \frac{d\Pi}{dQ} = MR - MC = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; MR = MC \]

Elasticity and markup, slides 555, 556, 562

\[ MR = P\left(1 - \frac{1}{|\varepsilon|}\right) \] \[ \frac{P - MC}{P} = \frac{1}{|\varepsilon|} \]
  • \(|\varepsilon| > 1\): \(MR > 0\). \(|\varepsilon| < 1\): \(MR < 0\). \(|\varepsilon| = 1\): \(MR = 0\), revenue is at its maximum.

Natural monopoly, slide 599

\[ TC = F + MQ \qquad ATC = \frac{F}{Q} + M > M = MC \] \[ P = M \;\Rightarrow\; \Pi = (M - ATC)\,Q = -F \]

Welfare, slide 596 (areas \(S_1\), \(S_2\), \(\Pi\))

\[ \text{competition: } S_1 + S_2 + \Pi \] \[ \text{monopoly: } S_2 + \Pi, \quad \text{loss: } S_1 \]

Derivation of \(MR\), of the elasticity form, and of the markup rule, plus an interactive monopoly graph with consumer surplus, profit, and deadweight loss: see 0.8.

ExampleMonopoly with linear demand

Slides 558 and 559: demand \(P = 100 - 2Q\), total cost \(TC = 640 + 20Q\), amounts in EUR.

  1. Revenue \(TR = 100Q - 2Q^2\), so \(MR = 100 - 4Q\). Marginal cost \(MC = 20\).
  2. \(MR = MC\): \(100 - 4Q = 20\), so \(Q^* = 20\).
  3. Price from the demand curve, not from \(MR\): \(P^* = 100 - 2\cdot 20 = 60\).
  4. Average cost: \(ATC = 640/20 + 20 = 52\).
  5. Profit: \((60 - 52)\cdot 20 = 160\). Check: \(TR = 1{,}200\), \(TC = 640 + 400 = 1{,}040\).

Markup check at the optimum

\[ \varepsilon = \frac{dQ}{dP}\cdot\frac{P}{Q} = -\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{60}{20} = -1.5 \] \[ \frac{P - MC}{P} = \frac{60 - 20}{60} = \frac{2}{3} = \frac{1}{1.5} \]

\(MR = 0\) at \(Q = 25\), the revenue maximum. The monopolist stays left of it, in the elastic part of demand. The cost function has the natural-monopoly form \(F + MQ\) with \(F = 640\), \(M = 20\).

PitfallsMonopoly traps
  • Price from demand, not from \(MR\): \(MR = MC\) gives the quantity. The price is the height of the demand curve at that quantity.
  • Profit maximum is not revenue maximum: revenue peaks where \(MR = 0\); profit peaks where \(MR = MC\), at a smaller quantity when \(MC > 0\) (slide 546).
  • Monopoly does not mean inelastic demand: the monopolist always operates in the elastic part of its demand curve (slide 561).
  • Deadweight loss bounds: the triangle runs from \(Q^*\) to \(Q_C\), between the demand curve and \(MC\), not \(MR\).
  • Profit is not the welfare loss: the profit rectangle is a transfer from consumers. Only the triangle \(S_1\) is lost (slide 596).
Macro linkMarkups in macro
  • Price-setting relation: in Blanchard and Illing firms set \(P = (1 + m)W\), a markup \(m\) over the marginal cost \(W\) (labor only, \(Y = N\)). From the markup rule here, \(1 + m = \frac{|\varepsilon|}{|\varepsilon| - 1}\). With \(|\varepsilon| = 2\), \(m = 1\): the price is twice marginal cost, as on slide 562.
  • Real wage and natural unemployment: price setting implies \(W/P = 1/(1 + m)\). Weaker product market competition, a higher \(m\), lowers the real wage and raises the natural rate of unemployment. Stronger competition works the other way.
  • New Keynesian models: firms in monopolistic competition set prices above marginal cost. Because \(P > MC\), they are happy to serve extra demand at an unchanged price, so with sticky prices output responds to demand in the short run.
  • Output too low: markups keep output below the efficient level, the economy-wide version of the deadweight loss on slide 596.
QuestionMicro 13.1

Slide 560: demand is still \(P = 100 - 2Q\), but total cost rises to \(TC = 640 + 40Q\). Find \(Q^*\), \(P^*\), and profit. Should the monopolist produce in the short run?

Show answer

\(MR = 100 - 4Q = 40\), so \(Q^* = 15\) and \(P^* = 100 - 30 = 70\).

Profit: \(TR = 70\cdot 15 = 1{,}050\), \(TC = 640 + 600 = 1{,}240\), so \(\Pi = -190\). Equivalently \(ATC = 640/15 + 40 \approx 82.67 > 70\).

In the short run it still produces: the price 70 exceeds \(AVC = 40\), and the loss of 190 is smaller than the 640 it would lose by shutting down. In the long run it would leave the market.

Compared with \(MC = 20\): marginal cost rose by 20, the price by only 10, and output fell from 20 to 15.

QuestionMicro 13.2

Use slide 558 (\(P = 100 - 2Q\), \(MC = 20\), monopoly at \(Q^* = 20\), \(P^* = 60\)). What quantity would \(P = MC\) give? How big are the deadweight loss and the consumer surplus under monopoly? What would a firm earn at \(P = MC\)?

Show answer

\(P = MC\): \(100 - 2Q = 20\), so \(Q_C = 40\).

Deadweight loss: the triangle between demand and \(MC\) from 20 to 40: \(\tfrac12\cdot(60 - 20)\cdot(40 - 20) = 400\).

Consumer surplus under monopoly: \(\tfrac12\cdot(100 - 60)\cdot 20 = 400\). At \(P = MC\) it would be \(\tfrac12\cdot(100 - 20)\cdot 40 = 1{,}600\).

At \(P = MC = 20\) the firm covers only marginal cost and loses its fixed cost of 640: the natural-monopoly problem from slide 599.

IdeaStrategic games and equilibrium
  • Why game theory (Spieltheorie): in perfect competition and monopoly a firm can ignore its rivals. In oligopoly and monopolistic competition each firm's best choice depends on what the others do (slide 607). Game theory studies such strategic interaction, slide 610.
  • Elements of a game (slide 615): players (Spieler), the strategies (Strategien) open to each, and the payoffs (Auszahlungen) for every combination of strategies, often shown in a payoff matrix (Auszahlungsmatrix). In each cell the first number belongs to the row player.
  • Dominant strategy (dominante Strategie), slide 617: best for a player whatever the others do. If every player has one, the result is an equilibrium in dominant strategies (Gleichgewicht in dominanten Strategien), slide 620.
  • Prisoner's dilemma (Gefangenendilemma), slides 613 to 619: confessing is dominant for each prisoner, yet both would be better off denying. Individually rational choices produce an outcome that is worse for both. Split or Steal (slides 611 and 612), cartels (slides 621 to 624), and advertising (slide 628) share this structure.
  • Nash equilibrium (Nash-Gleichgewicht), slide 630: a combination of strategies in which no player gains by switching, given the others' strategies. The strategies are mutual best responses. No dominant strategy is needed.
  • Slide 629: only firm 1 has a dominant strategy, advertising (750 > 500 and 300 > 200). Firm 2 anticipates this and advertises too (200 > 100). (Advertise, advertise) is the Nash equilibrium.
  • Dominant versus Nash (slide 631): a dominant strategy is best against everything the other player might do. A Nash strategy only has to be best against what the other player actually does. Every equilibrium in dominant strategies is a Nash equilibrium, but not the reverse.
IdeaRepeated games, sequential games, commitment
  • Repeated games (wiederholte Spiele): when the same players meet again and again, cooperation can pay. Tit-for-tat (Wie du mir, so ich dir), slide 625: cooperate in the first round, then copy what the other player did in the round before. The slide's condition: the number of future rounds is unknown.
  • Price-matching guarantees, slide 626: "we refund the difference plus 10 percent" looks like fierce competition. In fact it commits the firm to match any price cut at once, so rivals gain nothing by cutting. Prices can stay high: a form of tacit collusion (implizite Absprache).
  • Sequential games (sequentielle Spiele), slide 634: one player moves first, the other moves knowing that choice. Solve from the end by backward induction (Rückwärtsinduktion): find the last mover's best reply on each branch, then let the first mover choose knowing these replies.
  • Credible threats, slide 635: in the nuclear deterrence game, once the USSR has fired, the USA does better not to fire back (\(-50\) against \(-100\)). Foreseeing this, the USSR gets 100 from firing against 0 from not firing. A threat that would not be carried out deters no one.
  • Strategic deterrence (strategische Abschreckung), slides 636 and 637: on slide 636 the incumbent (the Shard) would not build higher after entry (40 against 30), so firm X enters and gets 60. On slide 637 building higher pays the incumbent (40 against 30). The threat is now credible, so X stays out (0 against \(-50\)) and the incumbent keeps 100.
  • Commitment through capacity, slide 638: a plant with very low marginal cost, even at higher total cost, signals that the incumbent can cut prices hard after entry. Entry stops being rational, and the incumbent keeps a high price.
FormulaEquilibrium conditions and recipe

Two players with strategies \(s_1\), \(s_2\) and payoffs \(\pi_1(s_1, s_2)\), \(\pi_2(s_1, s_2)\). The slides state the definitions in words; these are the usual symbols.

Dominant strategy \(s_1^d\) of player 1

\[ \pi_1(s_1^d, s_2) \ge \pi_1(s_1, s_2) \;\text{ for all } s_1, s_2 \]

Nash equilibrium \((s_1^*, s_2^*)\)

\[ \pi_1(s_1^*, s_2^*) \ge \pi_1(s_1, s_2^*) \;\text{ for all } s_1 \] \[ \pi_2(s_1^*, s_2^*) \ge \pi_2(s_1^*, s_2) \;\text{ for all } s_2 \]
  1. For each column, mark the row player's best payoff (first number).
  2. For each row, mark the column player's best payoff (second number).
  3. A cell with both marks is a Nash equilibrium.
  4. If all of the row player's marks lie in one row, that row is a dominant strategy. Same for the column player and one column.
  5. Sequential game: start at the last move, keep each mover's best branch, and work back to the first move.
ExampleWhy cartels are unstable

Slides 621 to 624: two firms sell mineral water at marginal cost 0. Market demand is \(P = 20 - Q\).

  1. Cartel: act like one monopolist. \(MR = 20 - 2Q = 0\) gives \(Q = 10\) and \(P = 10\). Each firm sells 5 and earns 50.
  2. Going it alone (Alleingang): cut the price to 9. Demand is 11, all of it at the deviator, so it earns 99 and the other firm 0.
  3. Both cut: they share 11 units at a price of 9, so each earns 49.5.
Firm 1 \ Firm 2Keep, \(P = 10\)Cut, \(P = 9\)
Keep the deal (Absprache einhalten)50, 500, 99
Cut (Alleingang)99, 049.5, 49.5
  • Cutting is dominant: 99 > 50 if the rival keeps the deal, 49.5 > 0 if it cuts.
  • Both cut and earn 49.5 instead of 50: a prisoner's dilemma.
  • It does not stop there: a lone cut to 8 sells 12 units and earns 96 (slide 624), and so on.
PitfallsReading payoff tables

Prisoner's dilemma, payoffs in years of prison as negative numbers (slides 614 and 619):

A \ BConfess (gestehen)Deny (leugnen)
Confess\(-3, -3\)\(0, -6\)
Deny\(-6, 0\)\(-1, -1\)
  • Bigger is better, even when negative: \(-3\) beats \(-6\), so confessing wins against both of B's choices.
  • Slide 619 says in its side text that each prisoner gets five years if both confess. The matrix on slides 614 and 619 and the text on slide 614 say three. This board uses three.
  • Slide 632 (Lufthansa and Alitalia) as printed: keeping advertising as before is dominant for both firms (8,000 > 5,500 and 6,000 > 2,000). The Nash equilibrium is (as before, as before) with 6,000 each, which is efficient. If the two off-diagonal cells were meant the other way round, raising advertising would be dominant and the game a prisoner's dilemma with 5,500 each. Check in the tutorial which version is intended.
  • Nash is not efficient by definition: in a prisoner's dilemma the equilibrium is worse for both players than another outcome.
  • "Dominant" belongs to one player's strategy, "equilibrium" to the combination of all players' strategies.
Macro linkGame theory in macro policy
  • Time inconsistency (Zeitinkonsistenz), Kydland and Prescott (1977): a central bank announces low inflation. Once wages are set, it is tempted to inflate to push unemployment down. Wage setters foresee this, so the announcement is not credible, like the threat in the deterrence game on slide 635.
  • Inflation bias, Barro and Gordon (1983): under discretion the equilibrium has higher inflation and no lower unemployment. A credible commitment to a rule does better.
  • Commitment devices: central bank independence, inflation targets, and appointing a conservative central banker change the policymaker's payoffs, just as the incumbent's investment on slide 637 makes its threat credible.
  • Reputation: the game is repeated, so a central bank can build credibility over time, the macro version of cooperation in repeated games (slide 625).
  • Games between policymakers: monetary and fiscal authorities, or governments of different countries choosing whether to stimulate demand, face the same strategic logic as the payoff tables here.
QuestionMicro 14.1

Slide 633, payoffs (Lufthansa, Alitalia): both raise advertising (4,000, 3,000); only Lufthansa raises (3,000, 8,000); only Alitalia raises (5,000, 4,000); neither raises (2,000, 5,000). Does either firm have a dominant strategy? Find the Nash equilibrium.

Show answer

Lufthansa: if Alitalia raises, keeping is better (5,000 > 4,000); if Alitalia keeps, raising is better (3,000 > 2,000). No dominant strategy.

Alitalia: if Lufthansa raises, keeping is better (8,000 > 3,000); if Lufthansa keeps, keeping is better (5,000 > 4,000). Keeping advertising as before is dominant.

Lufthansa anticipates that Alitalia keeps and raises its own advertising (3,000 > 2,000). Nash equilibrium: Lufthansa raises, Alitalia keeps, with payoffs (3,000, 8,000). Neither firm gains by switching alone.

QuestionMicro 14.2

Slides 636 and 637: firm X decides first whether to enter. After entry, the Shard decides whether to build higher. Slide 636 payoffs (Shard, X): higher (30, \(-50\)), not higher (40, 60), no entry (100, 0). On slide 637 the first two change to (40, \(-50\)) and (30, 60). Solve both games by backward induction.

Show answer

Slide 636: after entry the Shard compares 30 and 40 and does not build higher. X foresees this and compares 60 with 0, so it enters. Outcome: (40, 60). The Shard's threat to build higher is not credible.

Slide 637: after entry building higher pays the Shard (40 > 30). X foresees a payoff of \(-50\) and stays out (0 > \(-50\)). Outcome: (100, 0).

Changing its own payoffs in advance, by commitment, lets the incumbent deter entry: strategic deterrence.

GraphKinked budget sets: vouchers, discounts, and subsidies

Three budget sets (Budgetmengen, shaded) whose frontier has a kink (Knick). Drink vouchers (Getränkemarken): 100 euros, both prices 1, plus vouchers worth 40 that buy only drinks (slides 83 to 87). Quantity discount (Mengenrabatt): \(m = 100\), \(p_2 = 1\), and \(p_1 = 2\) for the first 20 units, then 1 (slides 88 to 93). Housing: income 500 euros per week, and the state gives 290 either as cash (Geldtransfer) or as a housing subsidy (Wohnkostenzuschuss) that can only pay rent (slides 202 to 209). In the housing case, \(U = X^aY^{1-a}\) and the share slider \(a\) are an own assumption, since the slides draw the curves without a formula. At \(a = 0.3\), \(J = (150, 350)\) is the choice without help, cash gives \(K = (237, 553)\), and the subsidy forces the corner \(D = (290, 500)\). The loss is small (the subsidy is worth 282.16 in cash, not 290); lower \(a\) to see a larger gap. From \(a = 290/790 \approx 0.367\) on, both give the same bundle (slide 207).

FormulaSlope of a level curve: GRS and TRS

Along an indifference curve utility stays the same, so its total differential is zero. Solve that for \(dx_2/dx_1\) and you get the slope, the Grenzrate der Substitution (GRS).

Utility constant: \(dU = 0\)

\[ dU = MU_1\,dx_1 + MU_2\,dx_2 = 0 \] \[ GRS = \frac{dx_2}{dx_1} = -\frac{MU_1}{MU_2} \]

Same rule for isoquants (TRS) and any level curve

\[ TRS = -\frac{MP_1}{MP_2} \qquad F(x, y) = c \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{F_x}{F_y} \]

Example (slide 182): \(U = x_1 x_2\) gives \(MU_1 = x_2\), \(MU_2 = x_1\), so \(GRS = -x_2/x_1\), which is \(-8\) at \((1, 8)\). The slides sometimes drop the minus sign and compare \(|GRS|\) with \(p_1/p_2\). Both say the same thing: at the optimum the indifference curve is as steep as the budget line.

FormulaMonotone transformations

A strictly increasing function \(f\) (for example \(\ln\), \(\sqrt{\ }\), \(U^2\), or \(2U + 10\)) keeps the ranking of all bundles. The indifference curves, the GRS, and the optimum stay the same.

Why the GRS does not change (chain rule)

\[ V = f(U), \quad f' > 0 \] \[ \frac{\partial V/\partial x_1}{\partial V/\partial x_2} = \frac{f'(U)\,MU_1}{f'(U)\,MU_2} = \frac{MU_1}{MU_2} \]

Log trick for Cobb-Douglas

\[ \ln\bigl(x_1^{c}\,x_2^{d}\bigr) = c\ln x_1 + d\ln x_2 \] \[ \bigl(x_1^{c}x_2^{d}\bigr)^{\frac{1}{c+d}} = x_1^{a}\,x_2^{1-a}, \quad a = \frac{c}{c+d} \]

Use the log form before taking derivatives: \(MU_1\) becomes \(c/x_1\), which is much easier to work with in the Lagrange conditions.

FormulaConsumer choice with Lagrange

Course form (slides 211 to 214)

\[ \max_{x_1, x_2, \lambda}\ L = U(x_1, x_2) - \lambda\,(p_1x_1 + p_2x_2 - m) \]

First-order conditions (BEO)

\[ (1)\ \ MU_1 - \lambda p_1 = 0 \qquad (2)\ \ MU_2 - \lambda p_2 = 0 \] \[ (3)\ \ m - p_1x_1 - p_2x_2 = 0 \] \[ (1) : (2) \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{MU_1}{MU_2} = \frac{p_1}{p_2} \]

Slide 214: \(U = x_1x_2\), \(p_1 = 4\), \(p_2 = 2\), \(m = 40\)

\[ \frac{x_2}{x_1} = \frac{4}{2} \Rightarrow x_2 = 2x_1, \quad 4x_1 + 2\cdot 2x_1 = 40 \] \[ x_1^* = 5,\quad x_2^* = 10,\quad U = 50 \]

Cobb-Douglas shortcut: income shares

\[ U = x_1^{a}x_2^{b} \;\Rightarrow\; x_1^* = \frac{a}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_1}, \quad x_2^* = \frac{b}{a+b}\cdot\frac{m}{p_2} \]

Cost minimization is written \(C = rK + wL + \lambda\,(F(K, L) - Q_0)\) (slide 487). The sign in front of \(\lambda\) does not change the solution. There \(L\) means labor, not the Lagrange function.

PitfallsKinks and corners: when the tangency rule fails

\(MU_1/MU_2 = p_1/p_2\) only finds the optimum for smooth, convex indifference curves with an interior solution. Three preference types in the course need a different approach.

  • Perfect substitutes \(U = a x_1 + b x_2\): the GRS is the constant \(-a/b\). Compare utility per euro. If \(a/p_1 > b/p_2\), buy only good 1: \(x_1^* = m/p_1\), \(x_2^* = 0\). That is a corner solution (Randlösung). If the two ratios are equal, every bundle on the budget line is optimal.
  • Perfect complements \(U = \min\{a x_1, x_2\}\): there is no derivative at the kink. The optimum sits on the kink, \(x_2 = a x_1\), so \(p_1x_1 + p_2 a x_1 = m\) and \(x_1^* = \dfrac{m}{p_1 + a p_2}\).
  • Quasi-linear \(U = v(x_1) + x_2\): the tangency \(v'(x_1) = p_1/p_2\) holds only if you can afford it. Example \(U = 4\sqrt{x_1} + x_2\), \(p_2 = 1\): \(2/\sqrt{x_1} = p_1\), so \(x_1^* = 4/p_1^2\), whatever the income (no income effect).

Corner condition instead of equality

\[ x_2^* = 0 \text{ is optimal if } \frac{MU_1}{MU_2} \ge \frac{p_1}{p_2} \text{ at } x_1 = \frac{m}{p_1} \]

Piecewise functions (abschnittsweise definiert) show up in the same chapters. A quantity discount gives a budget line with slope \(-2\) for \(0 \le x_1 \le 20\) and \(-1\) above 20 (slides 85 to 93). Demand for perfect substitutes jumps between \(m/p_1\) and 0.

FormulaHomogeneity and returns to scale

Homogeneous of degree \(k\) (homogen vom Grad \(k\))

\[ f(t x_1, t x_2) = t^{k}\,f(x_1, x_2) \quad \text{for all } t > 0 \]
  • \(k > 1\): increasing returns to scale (steigende Skalenerträge). \(k = 1\): constant. \(k < 1\): decreasing.
  • Cobb-Douglas \(f = A\,x_1^{a}x_2^{b}\): \(f(tx_1, tx_2) = t^{a+b} f\), so the degree is \(a + b\).
  • Slide 451: \(y = 2\,x_1^{1/3}x_2^{1/3}\) gives \(t^{2/3}\): decreasing returns to scale. \(y = x_1 + 3x_2\) and \(\min\{x_1, x_2\}\) have degree 1.
  • Do not confuse this with a falling marginal product, \(\partial^2 f/\partial x_1^2 < 0\). With \(a = b = 0.6\) each marginal product falls, yet returns to scale increase, because \(0.6 + 0.6 > 1\) (slide 452).

FormulaAverage and marginal cost

Course notation (slides 465 to 470)

\[ TC(Q) = FC + VC(Q) \qquad MC = \frac{dTC}{dQ} \approx \frac{\Delta TC}{\Delta Q} \] \[ AFC = \frac{FC}{Q} \qquad AVC = \frac{VC}{Q} \] \[ ATC = \frac{TC}{Q} = AFC + AVC \]

Derivative of an average (quotient rule)

\[ \frac{d}{dQ}\,\frac{TC(Q)}{Q} = \frac{MC\cdot Q - TC}{Q^2} = \frac{MC - ATC}{Q} \]
  • \(ATC\) falls while \(MC < ATC\) and rises while \(MC > ATC\). So \(MC\) cuts \(ATC\) at its minimum. The slides state this; the quotient rule shows why.
  • The same holds for \(AVC\). Fixed costs drop out of \(MC\).
  • Short run: produce where \(P = MC\) on the rising part of \(MC\), and only if \(P \ge \min AVC\) (Betriebsminimum). Profit is positive only if \(P > \min ATC\) (Betriebsoptimum).
  • The same idea for production (used on the Makro board): marginal product \(MP_L = \partial Y/\partial L\), average product \(AP_L = Y/L\). For Cobb-Douglas \(Y = AK^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}\): \(MP_L = (1-\alpha)\,Y/L\) and \(MP_K = \alpha\,Y/K\). The marginal product is a fixed share of the average product.
FormulaRevenue, marginal revenue, elasticity

Marginal revenue (Grenzerlös), product rule

\[ TR(Q) = P(Q)\cdot Q \;\Rightarrow\; MR = P + P'(Q)\cdot Q \]

Linear inverse demand: MR is twice as steep

\[ P = a - bQ \;\Rightarrow\; TR = aQ - bQ^2,\quad MR = a - 2bQ \]

MR and elasticity, profit-maximizing markup

\[ \varepsilon = \frac{dQ}{dP}\cdot\frac{P}{Q} \qquad MR = P\left(1 - \frac{1}{|\varepsilon|}\right) \] \[ MR = MC \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{P - MC}{P} = \frac{1}{|\varepsilon|} \]
  • Slide 545: \(TR = 80Q - 0.2Q^2\) gives \(MR = 80 - 0.4Q\).
  • On a linear demand curve the elasticity changes along the line: \(|\varepsilon| > 1\) above the midpoint, \(1\) at the midpoint, below 1 underneath. Revenue is highest where \(|\varepsilon| = 1\), which is where \(MR = 0\).
  • Slide 562: with \(\varepsilon = -2\) the markup is \(0.5\), so the price is twice marginal cost.
  • With straight lines, surplus areas are triangles and rectangles: \(\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot\text{base}\cdot\text{height}\). No integrals are needed.

FormulaExpected value, expected utility, risk

Lottery with outcomes \(c_1, c_2\) and probabilities \(\pi, 1 - \pi\)

\[ E[c] = \pi\,c_1 + (1 - \pi)\,c_2 \] \[ EU = \pi\,u(c_1) + (1 - \pi)\,u(c_2) \]

Certainty equivalent and risk premium

\[ u(CE) = EU \;\Rightarrow\; CE = u^{-1}(EU) \] \[ RP = E[c] - CE \]
  • Spread (Streuung): the variance \(Var(c) = \pi\,(c_1 - E[c])^2 + (1 - \pi)\,(c_2 - E[c])^2\) measures how far the outcomes lie from the expected value; its square root is the standard deviation. A risk-averse person dislikes spread: a lottery with the same expected value but outcomes further apart has a lower expected utility.
  • Risk averse (risikoavers): \(u\) concave, \(u'' < 0\). Then \(u(E[c]) > EU\): the chord between two points lies below the curve. The risk premium is positive.
  • Risk neutral: \(u\) linear, \(CE = E[c]\). Risk loving (risikofreudig): \(u\) convex, \(CE > E[c]\).
  • To get \(CE\), invert \(u\): for \(u = \sqrt{c}\), \(CE = EU^2\). For \(u = \ln c\), \(CE = e^{EU}\).
  • A risk-averse person facing actuarially fair insurance (premium rate \(\gamma = \pi\)) insures fully (slides 419 to 423).

FormulaSolving for a variable inside a power

Isolate the power, then use the reciprocal exponent

\[ x^{a} = c \;\Rightarrow\; x = c^{1/a} \qquad \sqrt{x} = c \;\Rightarrow\; x = c^2 \]

Quasi-linear demand

\[ \frac{2}{\sqrt{x_1}} = p_1 \;\Rightarrow\; \sqrt{x_1} = \frac{2}{p_1} \;\Rightarrow\; x_1 = \frac{4}{p_1^2} \]

Compensating variation (slides 372 to 375)

\[ U = \sqrt{x_1x_2}:\quad x_1 = \frac{m}{2p_1},\ \ x_2 = \frac{m}{2p_2} \] \[ \Rightarrow\; U = \frac{m}{2\sqrt{p_1p_2}} \] \[ \frac{m''}{2\sqrt{2 \cdot 1}} = 50 \;\Rightarrow\; m'' = 100\sqrt{2} = 141.42 \]

With \(m = 100\) and \(p_1\) rising from 1 to 2, the old utility is 50, so \(CV = 141.42 - 100 = 41.42\). When the unknown is in the exponent instead, take logs (see 0.1).

FormulaAdding demand curves and piecewise functions

Market demand adds quantities at the same price, not prices. Solve each inverse demand for \(Q\), add, then solve back for \(P\).

Slides 278 and 279

\[ P = 30 - 2Q_D \;\Rightarrow\; Q_D = 15 - \tfrac{1}{2}P \] \[ P = 30 - 3Q_R \;\Rightarrow\; Q_R = 10 - \tfrac{1}{3}P \] \[ Q = 25 - \tfrac{5}{6}P \;\Rightarrow\; P = 30 - 1.2\,Q \]

Different intercepts give a kink (abschnittsweise Funktion)

\[ Q_A = 20 - P, \qquad Q_B = 10 - P \] \[ Q(P) = \begin{cases} 30 - 2P & 0 \le P \le 10 \\ 20 - P & 10 < P \le 20 \\ 0 & P > 20 \end{cases} \]
  • Identical firms (slides 526 and 527): 200 firms with \(P = 100 + 1000\,q_i\) give \(q_i = (P - 100)/1000\), so \(Q = 200\,q_i\) and \(P = 100 + 5Q\).
  • Piecewise rules also appear in the monopoly with a world market (slide 572): \(MR = MR_{\text{home}}\) while it is above the world price 12, and 12 below that.
FormulaReaction functions and backward induction

Oligopoly tasks are systems of equations. Take each firm's partial derivative while treating the other firm's quantity as a constant, then solve by substitution (Einsetzungsverfahren).

Cournot, \(P = 56 - 2(Q_1 + Q_2)\), \(MC = 20\) (slides 642 to 650)

\[ \Pi_1 = (56 - 2Q_1 - 2Q_2)\,Q_1 - 20\,Q_1 \] \[ \frac{\partial \Pi_1}{\partial Q_1} = 36 - 4Q_1 - 2Q_2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; Q_1 = 9 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q_2 \]

Use symmetry: \(Q_1 = Q_2 = Q\)

\[ Q = 9 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q \;\Rightarrow\; Q = 6, \quad P = 56 - 2\cdot 12 = 32 \]

Stackelberg: solve the follower first, then substitute

\[ P = 56 - 2Q_1 - 2\left(9 - \tfrac{1}{2}Q_1\right) = 38 - Q_1 \] \[ MR_1 = 38 - 2Q_1 = 20 \;\Rightarrow\; Q_1 = 9,\ Q_2 = 4.5,\ P = 29 \]

General Cournot with \(P = a - b(Q_1 + Q_2)\), \(MC = c\)

\[ Q_1 = \frac{a - c - bQ_2}{2b} \qquad Q_1 = Q_2 = \frac{a - c}{3b} \]

Solving the last stage first and working backward is called backward induction (Rückwärtsinduktion). The slides do the same in the game trees (slides 635 to 637) without naming it. Bertrand drives the price down to \(P = MC = 20\).
